#9772. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

#9770. llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

#9768. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

#9767. The Benefits and Risks of Updating Multiple Programs Through a Shared Handler

Founder and chief engineer at Extella (https://extella.dev). Named inventor on U.S. patents in computing architecture.

Founder and chief engineer at Extella (https://extella.dev). Named inventor on U.S. patents in computing architecture.

Founder and chief engineer at Extella (https://extella.dev). Named inventor on U.S. patents in computing architecture.

For developers maintaining internal tools: changing shared rules in reports and calculations, checking the results, and restoring previous behavior.

We updated one shared handler in Extella and changed the formatting and validation rules of 40 report programs on their next run, without modifying their source code. When we deliberately introduced an error, a validation check detected incorrect totals in 35 of the reports and blocked the update. After we bypassed the check to test recovery, restoring the previous handler brought all 40 reports back to their correct totals.

The approach puts shared logic in a handler: code that executes commands written in a small language for a particular task. Each program describes what needs to be done, while the handler takes care of execution. Libraries and services also let programs share logic; here we examine what this arrangement requires in practice.

The experiment showed both sides of shared execution: one update can change multiple programs at once, but one error can affect many of them.

For a developer maintaining these programs, the next question is how to test a shared change and restore the previous behavior if it goes wrong. We follow those steps below, then examine a separate experiment in which an AI model uses prepared commands to write new programs.

Changing shared rules separately from a report requires separating two parts of the program. The report description holds data and commands. The handler holds the calculation, formatting, and validation code. A small language with commands for a particular set of tasks is called a domain-specific language, or DSL.

The first handler needs to be written and tested against examples with known results. The developer also defines which commands it supports and what each one means. If those commands cover a new report’s requirements, its author can specify the data and commands using the calculation and validation code already in the handler.

A familiar analogy is a template engine: a template specifies fields and placeholders, and the engine turns them into a finished page. Here, too, the report description is separate from the code that executes it. Changing the shared formatting code changes how reports look on subsequent runs (Scheme 1).

It performs shared calculations, validation, and formatting. After an update, programs apply the new rules on subsequent runs without source changes, provided the handler remains compatible with the existing commands.

A short example shows exactly what stays in a program when its handler changes. In the ledger language, add N adds a number to the total and sub N subtracts one. A Python handler was tested with four saved programs. One looked like this:

Starting at zero, the handler calculates 5 + 7 − 2 = 10. The first version returned the total; the second added the number of commands and the largest number specified. The total calculation stayed the same.

After the handler was replaced, all four programs returned their previous totals with new response fields. Their source text was neither changed nor saved again.

This is backward-compatible for an application that reads only the total field. A strict check of the field set could reject the new response. That would require preserving the old format or updating dependent programs.

At this point, a developer might ask why a custom language is needed when shared code can already live in a function, library, or service. A Python function is indeed enough for two arithmetic commands. Ledger shows how to separate a program from its execution; this example establishes no advantage over an ordinary function.

In our comparisons, an ordinary script called programs through MCP (Model Context Protocol), an interface for connecting tools. MCP provided the call interface; no AI model chose the actions. A simple MCP server could also store and run programs. Windmill, a script-running environment, provided version history and rollback; it was tested on one machine.

The next test therefore follows a shared change through a set of reports: applying it, detecting a defect, and restoring the previous results. That requires an expected total for each report.

The main experiment used 40 small report programs containing different sets of amounts. The shared handler was updated to format totals and reject duplicate row names. All 40 programs used the new rules on subsequent runs without source changes. The developer could maintain these rules in one place while each report kept its own data and commands. The next step was to check the results across all 40 reports.

We then tested what would happen if the shared update were wrong. A deliberately faulty version dropped the fractional part of each row's amount before adding the amounts together. Before installing it, a separate validation program compared the results with values calculated in advance. It found 35 incorrect totals out of 40 and rejected the update. The previous handler remained in place and continued to produce 40 correct totals.

Directly registering the handler could bypass this check. The experiment did exactly that: it installed the faulty version, obtained incorrect totals, then restored the previous version and recovered all 40 correct results.

The check worked because correct totals were already known for all 40 programs. Recovery used a saved copy of the previous handler, registered again after the faulty update.

The 40-report experiment tested updating and recovery; it did not compare maintenance costs with a library or service. A separate test changed the appearance of one report and showed no time or token savings. Each approach was tried once.

Checking totals is not enough when reports run on different devices. The new handler also has to run in each environment. Each device needs a runner, the appropriate handler version, and the dependencies it uses. Before updating, check the environment and run validation programs on each device. Saving the new source code alone does not establish that these requirements are met.

A separate experiment examines dependencies and code delivery on two devices. It updated a saved calculation operation while leaving the language handlers unchanged. It helps explain deployment requirements, but does not test replacing a shared handler.

So far, we have examined changes to programs that already work. The prepared handler can also serve the next program: a person or an AI model describes the task using its commands. The model can draw on operations whose execution and checks have already been implemented. To find out whether such commands help a model, we ran a separate employee-scheduling experiment comparing schedule correctness and token use.

The model wrote either a Python program that produced a schedule or commands in a scheduling language. Prewritten code checked hours and constraints, such as whether enough employees were available at a given time. Both formats used the same rules; in the DSL version, the checks were part of the handler and made no AI calls.

Three approaches were compared on six tasks using qwen-flash. Each task was repeated three times for each approach, giving 18 task runs per approach. In the approaches with feedback, a run allowed up to three attempts: after an error, the model received feedback and could revise its program.

In the last two approaches, the model received the same general rules and up to three attempts. Python with revisions used about 5.7 times as many tokens as the scheduling DSL. These totals include both successful and unsuccessful task runs. Eight DSL runs still failed validation. In two cases, Python with revisions passed while the scheduling DSL failed.

With the stronger qwen3.7-max-2026-06-08 model, each task was run once per approach. All three approaches passed all six tasks, and the scheduling DSL had no token advantage. These results come from saved logs. The logs do not include the models' final programs, so they cannot be used to independently rerun every generated schedule.

These results concern a model using commands that are already available. The token totals exclude developing and testing the handler. They compare the scheduling approach as a whole, including the language, execution, and feedback. They do not measure the cost of updating reports. A stronger model could help write a handler for a smaller model to use, but the experiment did not measure the full cost of that workflow.

The report experiment checked totals, while the scheduling experiment checked constraints. A working system also needs compatibility with applications that consume the programs' output. A breaking change to that output requires preserving the previous format or updating dependent applications.

Recovery needs a saved working handler and a way to restore it even if the new version is broken. Restoring the code does not undo completed actions, such as an email already sent. Built-in version history and updates during running calls were not tested.

The checking code can also be wrong. The first schedule validator missed a five-minute gap; this article uses the corrected experiment. The checks therefore need tests with valid and invalid inputs. Changes to the checking code, including changes made by an agent, need review separately from changes to the program being checked.

The execution path can add latency. A separate comparison made 30 repeated calls per method. The medians were about 9.4 seconds through the program-execution service and 0.025 seconds through a simple local runner. Computation ran on the same laptop, but the call paths differed; this does not isolate the cost of the language itself.

Checks in the handler help find errors in a program, but do not restrict the handler’s own permissions. In the configuration described here, the handler runs with the user’s permissions, so access to files, the network, and system commands needs separate restrictions.

A handler is worth considering when several tasks use a stable set of operations. Reports may contain different data while calculating and displaying totals according to shared rules. A new report can then use existing commands. When a shared rule changes, the developer updates the handler and checks every affected report.

The initial preparation falls to whoever first defines the commands, writes the handler, and tests it. Other people and AI models can then compose programs from those operations, reusing the code that executes and checks them. The developer still needs to check that each program meets its requirements. A task outside the supported operations requires extending the handler and testing it again.

A library or service also supports shared code. The choice depends on how well a separate language expresses your tasks and whether reuse justifies maintaining it. Compare the full cycle: building the handler, adding programs, changing shared rules, checking results, and recovering from errors. For one report, this extra work may be unnecessary.

We ran these experiments, calling this mechanism CSPL (Container Specific Programming Language): each saved program specifies its language, and a handler registered on the device executes its commands. The code, Erun logs, and results of the 40-report and scheduling experiments are available on GitHub.

To assess the approach for your own tools, choose a small set of programs that share rules. Establish their expected results, change one rule, and check whether you can both apply and reverse the change. Account for writing the handler and maintaining those checks before deciding whether a custom language is worth keeping.

Founder and chief engineer at Extella (https://extella.dev). Named inventor on U.S. patents in computing architecture.

#9765. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo or Maziyar Panahi’s Microduck simulation. Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.

#9763. Apa Itu Lean 4? Pemeriksa Bukti di Balik Pembuktian Riemann Claude

Posted on Nov 23 • Originally published at apidog.com

Apa itu Lean 4? Lean 4 adalah bahasa pemrograman sekaligus asisten pembuktian sumber terbuka yang memeriksa bukti matematika dan properti program langkah demi langkah, dengan kernel tepercaya yang kecil yang menerima atau menolak setiap inferensi. Inilah alat yang dipakai peneliti Anthropic, Levent Alpöge, pada November 2026 untuk merilis bukti terverifikasi mesin—dibangun bersama Claude—yang menurutnya menyelesaikan hipotesis Riemann yang digeneralisasi.

Panduan ini menjelaskan bagaimana pemeriksa bukti Lean memutuskan apa yang benar, apa yang ditunjukkan dan tidak ditunjukkan oleh klaim Riemann tersebut, serta bagaimana menjalankan pembuktian pertama Anda.

Lean 4 adalah bahasa pemrograman fungsional dan pembuktian teorema interaktif. Anda menyatakan sebuah teorema sebagai tipe, menulis buktinya sebagai program bertipe tersebut, lalu kernel Lean memeriksa setiap langkahnya. Jika kernel menerimanya, bukti itu benar relatif terhadap logika dan aksioma Lean. Jika ada satu langkah saja yang gagal, berkasnya tidak akan terkompilasi.

Beberapa fakta dari halaman riwayat resmi Lean FRO:

Lean menyatukan dua alat sekaligus: bahasa yang dikompilasi ke kode native, dan asisten pembuktian dengan sistem tipe dependen yang memungkinkan Anda membuktikan bahwa kode memenuhi spesifikasinya untuk setiap input, bukan hanya input yang Anda uji.

Pada Jumat, 20 November 2026, Levent Alpöge, anggota staf teknis Anthropic, mengunggah catatan empat halaman di situs webnya: "Saya percaya saya telah, bersama Claude, menemukan bukti Hipotesis Riemann." Ia tidak menerbitkan makalah konvensional. Ia merilis argumennya sebagai kode Lean, demikian laporan Al Jazeera, dan menulis bahwa "Claude jauh melampaui saya menjelang garis finis."

Pahami dulu cakupannya, karena banyak judul berita keliru:

Mengapa Lean penting di sini? Tidak ada yang sanggup membaca 17 juta baris. Klaim ini layak diperhatikan justru karena sebuah program kecil yang sudah banyak diteliti telah memeriksa setiap barisnya.

Lean memisahkan tugasnya menjadi front end yang tidak tepercaya dan back end yang tepercaya. Semua kecerdasan terjadi di front end. Semua yang harus Anda percayai berada di kernel, yang oleh situs Lean disebut sebagai "kernel tepercaya yang minimal."

Berikut alur pipa tersebut secara berurutan:

Inilah alasan bukti yang ditulis AI bisa dipercaya: sebagian besar upaya salah, dan hanya term yang diterima kernel yang bertahan.

Ada dua celah yang perlu diperhatikan. sorry memungkinkan Anda melewati satu langkah, dan Lean menandai setiap deklarasi yang memakainya. Aksioma tambahan memungkinkan Anda mengasumsikan sesuatu. Perintah #print axioms mencantumkan setiap aksioma yang menjadi landasan sebuah teorema, sehingga peninjau bisa melihat dalam satu baris apakah ada hal yang diasumsikan.

Berikut berkas Lean 4 lengkap yang bisa Anda tempel ke Lean playground:

Peninjau sebuah hasil besar memeriksa hal ini lebih dulu: tidak ada sorry, tidak ada aksioma tak terduga.

Pembuktian teorema oleh AI berjalan sebagai sebuah lingkaran. Model mengusulkan, Lean menjawab, model mencoba lagi. Kesalahan dan tujuan yang belum tertutup dari Lean menjadi umpan baliknya; putusan kernel bersifat final.

Pola ini sama dengan yang mendasari karya-karya sebelumnya yang mungkin sudah Anda baca. AlphaProof dari Google DeepMind mencapai performa medali perak IMO pada Juli 2024 menggunakan Lean dan Mathlib, dan model terbuka seperti DeepSeek Prover V2 serta DeepSeekMath-V2 dilatih dengan Lean atau memverifikasi langkahnya sendiri.

Mathlib adalah alasan pendekatan ini bisa berkembang. Situs Lean menyebutnya sebagai pustaka komunitas berisi "lebih dari satu juta baris matematika terformalisasi" yang mencakup aljabar, analisis, topologi, dan probabilitas. Pembuktian tentang fungsi L tidak dimulai dari aksioma aritmetika; ia dibangun di atas apa yang sudah diperiksa Mathlib.

Para pengembang mengenal versi lebih lemah dari gagasan ini: pengujian.

Sebuah bukti bisa sempurna namun tetap membuktikan pernyataan yang keliru, itulah sebabnya para matematikawan akan menghabiskan berminggu-minggu membaca apa yang sebenarnya dinyatakan oleh kode Lean Alpöge. Pengujian membuktikan lebih sedikit, tetapi murah dan dijalankan pada setiap commit.

Untuk pemasangan lokal, ikuti panduan pemasangan manual resmi:

Pelajaran Lean bagi tim API sederhana: tuliskan kontraknya, lalu biarkan mesin memeriksa setiap hasil terhadap kontrak tersebut. Dalam pekerjaan API, kontraknya adalah spesifikasi Anda, dan pemeriksaannya adalah validasi respons.

Apidog memvalidasi respons terhadap skema yang dideklarasikan spesifikasi endpoint Anda, sehingga field yang hilang, tipe yang salah, dan properti tambahan langsung terlihat tanpa asersi yang ditulis manual. Apidog CLI memungkinkan coding agent Anda menjalankan pemeriksaan itu untuk Anda, sama seperti Claude menjalankan Lean dalam sebuah lingkaran. Anda menulis satu prompt; agent membaca spesifikasi, menulis kasus uji, dan menjalankannya.

Lalu berikan satu prompt kepada Claude Code, Codex, atau Cursor:

Agent akan mencari endpoint dan respons yang dideklarasikannya, menulis kasus uji berdasarkan skema yang tervalidasi, lalu menjalankan setiap kasus pada endpoint tersebut:

Seperti kernel Lean, spesifikasi adalah wasitnya: ketika backend menyimpang, proses run gagal dan agent memberi tahu Anda field mana yang bermasalah. Letakkan perintah test-case run ... -r junit yang sama di CI agar setiap pull request diperiksa; panduan CI/CD Apidog CLI menunjukkan penyiapan GitHub Actions, dan Apidog CLI di Claude Code membahas sisi agent-nya. Untuk teori pengujian di baliknya, lihat pengujian kontrak API. Paket Free Apidog mencakup hingga 4 pengguna.

Lean 4 digunakan untuk apa? Lean 4 digunakan untuk memformalkan matematika (Mathlib, proyek Teorema Terakhir Fermat), memverifikasi perangkat lunak dan perangkat keras, serta sebagai pemeriksa dalam pembuktian teorema oleh AI. Lean juga merupakan bahasa fungsional serbaguna yang dikompilasi ke kode native.

Apakah Claude membuktikan hipotesis Riemann? Levent Alpöge menyatakan bahwa ia menemukan bukti hipotesis Riemann yang digeneralisasi saat bekerja dengan Claude dan merilisnya sebagai kode Lean. Lean telah memeriksa kodenya; para matematikawan masih menelusuri apa yang ditunjukkan oleh 17 juta baris tersebut, yang diperkirakan memakan waktu berminggu-minggu.

Apakah Lean 4 gratis? Ya. Lean 4 dan Mathlib bersifat sumber terbuka, dan Lean FRO adalah organisasi nirlaba. Anda dapat menjalankannya secara lokal dengan elan atau di playground peramban tanpa biaya.

Bisakah pemeriksa bukti keliru? Secara prinsip bisa, itulah sebabnya Lean menjaga kernel tepercayanya tetap kecil dan mendukung pemeriksaan ulang independen dengan alat seperti Comparator. Risiko praktis yang lebih besar justru adalah pernyataan teorema yang tidak menyatakan maksud Anda.

Apakah saya perlu menguasai matematika lanjutan untuk belajar Lean 4? Tidak. Mulailah dengan teorema sederhana tentang bilangan asli dan list, atau dengan Lean sebagai bahasa pemrograman. Proyek tutorial Mathlib dan playground dirancang untuk pemula.

#9762. How to Install Claude Code on Android With Termux

AI coding agents are no longer limited to desktop computers.

With the right setup, you can run tools such as Claude Code directly on an Android phone using Termux. You do not need root access, a PC, or an Android emulator. This guide will show you how to set up Claude Code on Termux, explain two different installation paths, and cover some of the problems you may run into along the way.

The recommended approach uses Ubuntu inside Termux with proot-distro. It takes more storage than a native installation, but it gives the coding agent a more familiar Linux environment.

An AI coding agent is more than a chatbot that gives you code snippets.

A coding agent can work with files on your device, inspect an existing project, modify code, run commands, and help troubleshoot problems.

you can give the agent an existing project and ask it to inspect the code, make the required changes, and test the result.

Claude Code is one example of this type of tool. There are also other CLI-based coding agents that can be used from a Linux terminal.

On Android, Termux provides the terminal environment that makes this possible.

Before starting, check a few things first.

Your Android operating system needs to run on aarch64.

This is important because having a 64-bit ARM processor does not always mean that Android itself is running as a 64-bit operating system.

Some older or budget Android phones, including certain Samsung A-series devices, have shipped with a 32-bit Android OS even though their hardware is capable of 64-bit operation.

If uname -m returns something such as armv7l, this setup will not work as described here.

Install Termux from a current supported source such.

The Google Play situation has changed over time, but the Play Store build and the main Termux project have been separate, so using the established F-Droid/GitHub sources avoids mixing incompatible builds and packages.

You will need access to Claude if you are using Claude Code directly.

Authentication normally happens when you first start Claude Code.

The native route uses considerably less storage.

The Ubuntu route is heavier. Keep roughly 2 GB or more of free space available so the container and its packages have room to install properly.

There are two practical approaches worth knowing about.

The first approach runs the Linux ARM64 Claude Code binary directly through a compatibility layer in Termux.

It is attractive because the installation is smaller and you do not need an Ubuntu container.

However, this is not official Android support. Claude Code is distributed as a Linux binary, while Android uses the Bionic C library rather than the glibc environment expected by that binary.

Current community installers work around this by using tools such as glibc-runner and patching the binary's Linux interpreter.

There has also been a period where newer Claude Code releases broke older native Termux installation methods because the package moved to platform-specific native binaries.

Older guides often solved this by pinning Claude Code to version 2.1.112. Newer compatibility workarounds now exist, but the important point is that native Termux support is still a compatibility solution rather than an official Android build.

So if you see an older guide telling you to pin the Claude Code version, that advice comes from a real compatibility problem. It is not necessarily the only solution anymore.

The second approach places Ubuntu inside Termux.

proot-distro provides a Linux userland without requiring root access or a separate virtual machine.

This is the approach recommended in this guide.

The main advantage is that Claude Code sees a normal Linux environment instead of trying to operate directly against Android's userland.

It also gives you a useful Linux environment for other development tools.

There is a third option as well: Android Virtualization Framework (AVF) can provide a real Linux virtual machine on some newer devices. Current community documentation lists Pixel 6-class and newer supported devices as an experimental route. That setup is outside the scope of this guide.

proot-distro is what we will use to install and enter Ubuntu without root access.

Once the installation finishes, enter Ubuntu:

Your prompt should change to something similar to:

You are now inside the Ubuntu environment.

Your Ubuntu filesystem remains available between sessions.

Inside Ubuntu, update the package lists and installed packages:

This is worth doing before installing Claude Code because a fresh Ubuntu container may not have the latest packages and certificates required for downloads.

Current Claude Code documentation provides an official installer for Linux:

Anthropic's current documentation also supports an npm installation for Linux systems with Node.js, but the native installer is the simpler route here.

If the installer tells you that claude cannot be found, add its directory to your PATH:

If everything is working, you should get the installed Claude Code version. A common mistake here is trying to run claude immediately from a non-interactive shell before .bashrc has been loaded.

or starting a normal login shell solves that in most cases.

The first launch will ask you to authenticate. Depending on your Android version and browser setup, the authentication page may open automatically. On some older Android versions, you may need to copy the URL shown in the terminal and open it manually. Once authentication is complete, Claude Code can work with the files in your current project directory.

Suppose you have a Python project in your Ubuntu home directory.

From there, you can ask it to inspect the project, create files, explain existing code, or make changes.

The important difference from a normal AI chat is that the agent can work with the project itself rather than only seeing the code you manually paste into a conversation.

The setup is fairly straightforward, but Termux and Android introduce a few things that can be confusing.

One problem reported with native Termux installations involves DNS resolution. Android does not provide the normal Linux /etc/resolv.conf environment that many Linux programs expect. Some Linux binaries rely on a DNS resolver that reads this file, and when it is missing, they can fall back to a resolver address where nothing is listening.

This can result in connection attempts hanging or timing out. This is another reason the Ubuntu route is useful. If you encounter this problem on a native installation, check the documentation for the specific Termux/Claude compatibility layer you installed rather than randomly changing DNS settings.

Some current native installers include their own DNS workaround for affected devices.

If Claude installed successfully but the command cannot be found, check your PATH:

If you are using the native Termux route and Claude suddenly stops working after an update, check the version and the installation method you are using.

This has happened because Claude Code changed its binary distribution and older Termux workarounds were no longer compatible with newer releases.

If you want the least amount of troubleshooting, the Ubuntu route avoids much of this native Android compatibility layer.

Once everything is installed, you do not need to repeat the setup.

If you want to continue an existing Claude Code session, use the session commands supported by your installed Claude Code version.

If you are using a local routing proxy or another service outside Ubuntu, you may instead use two Termux sessions: one session keeps the routing service running while the other enters Ubuntu and runs Claude Code. For direct Claude API access, you can keep things much simpler and use a single Ubuntu session.

There is another setup that some Termux users experiment with.

A local AI router can sit between Claude Code and the model provider:

If a routing method depends on a provider's free tier or a third-party proxy, check the provider's current terms before relying on it.

Running an AI coding agent on a phone is useful, but a phone is still a phone.

AI coding agents can run commands, inspect files, and perform repeated operations.

Long sessions can therefore consume battery and generate heat, especially on less powerful phones.

Some Android manufacturers are aggressive about stopping background applications.

If you leave a long-running process in Termux and switch to another application, Android may eventually terminate it.

Battery optimization settings can also affect Termux.

proot-distro does not give you actual root privileges.

It creates a Linux-like environment in userspace. That is enough for many development tasks, but it does not provide the same control as a rooted Android device or a real Linux machine.

Termux, Android, Linux packages, and AI coding tools are all changing.

An update can occasionally introduce compatibility problems.

This is especially important with native Termux installations because they depend on compatibility layers between Android and Linux binaries.

The Ubuntu approach reduces some of those problems, but it does not eliminate them completely.

You do not need a PC to experiment with AI coding agents anymore. With Termux and proot-distro, an Android phone can provide a surprisingly capable Linux development environment.

For the setup covered here, Ubuntu inside Termux is the route to start with. It gives Claude Code a conventional Linux environment and avoids many of the compatibility problems that can appear when trying to run Linux binaries directly against Android.

The native Termux approach is still interesting if you want a smaller setup and are comfortable dealing with compatibility workarounds.

But whichever route you choose, the basic idea is simple:

Once that is working, your phone becomes more than a terminal for running commands. It can become a small development environment that you can carry around with you.

#9761. Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

#9760. ¿Qué es Lean 4? El verificador de demostraciones detrás de la prueba de Riemann de Claude

Posted on Nov 23 • Originally published at apidog.com

¿Qué es Lean 4? Lean 4 es un lenguaje de programación de código abierto que también funciona como asistente de demostración: comprueba paso a paso demostraciones matemáticas y propiedades de programas, con un kernel de confianza reducido que acepta o rechaza cada inferencia. Es la herramienta que el investigador de Anthropic Levent Alpöge utilizó en noviembre de 2026 para publicar una demostración verificada por máquina, construida con Claude, con la que asegura haber resuelto la hipótesis de Riemann generalizada.

Esta guía explica cómo decide el comprobador de demostraciones de Lean qué es verdadero, qué demuestra y qué no demuestra la afirmación sobre Riemann, y cómo ejecutar tu primera demostración.

Lean 4 es un lenguaje de programación funcional y un demostrador de teoremas interactivo. Enuncias un teorema como un tipo, escribes una demostración como un programa de ese tipo y el kernel de Lean comprueba cada paso. Si el kernel la acepta, la demostración es correcta en relación con la lógica y los axiomas de Lean. Si falla algún paso, el archivo no compila.

Algunos datos tomados de la página oficial de historia del Lean FRO:

Lean son dos herramientas en una: un lenguaje que compila a código nativo y un asistente de demostración cuyo sistema de tipos dependientes te permite demostrar que el código cumple su especificación para todas las entradas posibles, no solo para las que has probado.

El viernes 20 de noviembre de 2026, Levent Alpöge, miembro del equipo técnico de Anthropic, publicó una nota de cuatro páginas en su sitio web: «Creo que, trabajando con Claude, he descubierto una demostración de la hipótesis de Riemann». No publicó un artículo convencional. Presentó el argumento como código Lean, según informó Al Jazeera, y escribió que «Claude me superó con creces cerca de la meta».

Conviene precisar el alcance, porque muchos titulares no lo hacen:

¿Por qué importa Lean aquí? Nadie puede leer 17 millones de líneas. La afirmación merece atención porque un programa pequeño y ampliamente estudiado ya las ha comprobado todas.

Lean divide el trabajo en un front end no confiable y un back end confiable. Todo lo ingenioso ocurre en el front end. Todo aquello en lo que debes confiar vive en el kernel, que el sitio de Lean describe como un «kernel de confianza mínimo».

Por eso se puede confiar en una demostración escrita por una IA: la mayoría de los intentos son erróneos y solo sobreviven los términos que el kernel acepta.

Hay dos vías de escape que conviene tener en cuenta. sorry te permite saltarte un paso, y Lean marca cada declaración que lo usa. Los axiomas adicionales te permiten dar cosas por supuestas. El comando #print axioms enumera todos los axiomas de los que depende un teorema, de modo que quien lo revise puede ver en una sola línea si se ha asumido algo.

Aquí tienes un archivo Lean 4 completo que puedes pegar en el playground de Lean:

Quienes revisan un resultado importante comprueban esto primero: ningún sorry, ningún axioma inesperado.

La demostración automática de teoremas con IA funciona en bucle. El modelo propone, Lean responde, el modelo lo intenta de nuevo. Los errores y los objetivos abiertos de Lean son la retroalimentación; el veredicto del kernel es definitivo.

Este es el mismo patrón que hay detrás de trabajos anteriores de los que quizá hayas leído. AlphaProof de Google DeepMind alcanzó en julio de 2024 un rendimiento de medalla de plata en la OMI usando Lean y Mathlib, y modelos abiertos como DeepSeek Prover V2 y DeepSeekMath-V2 se entrenan con Lean o autoverifican sus propios pasos.

Mathlib es la razón de que esto pueda escalar. El sitio de Lean la describe como una biblioteca comunitaria de «más de un millón de líneas de matemáticas formalizadas» que abarca álgebra, análisis, topología y probabilidad. Una demostración sobre funciones L no parte de los axiomas de la aritmética, sino de lo que Mathlib ya ha comprobado.

Los desarrolladores conocen una versión más débil de esta idea: los tests.

Una demostración puede ser perfecta y aun así demostrar el enunciado equivocado, y por eso los matemáticos dedicarán semanas a leer qué afirman exactamente el código Lean de Alpöge. Un test demuestra menos, pero es barato y se ejecuta en cada commit.

Para instalarlo en local, sigue la guía oficial de instalación manual:

La lección de Lean para los equipos de API es sencilla: escribe el contrato y deja que una máquina compruebe cada resultado contra él. En el trabajo con APIs, el contrato es tu especificación y la comprobación es la validación de respuestas.

Apidog valida una respuesta contra el esquema que declara la especificación de tu endpoint, de modo que los campos que faltan, los tipos incorrectos y las propiedades de más aparecen sin necesidad de escribir aserciones a mano. Apidog CLI permite que tu agente de código ejecute esas comprobaciones por ti, igual que Claude ejecutaba Lean en bucle. Tú escribes un prompt; el agente lee la especificación, escribe los casos de prueba y los ejecuta.

Después, dale un prompt a Claude Code, Codex o Cursor:

El agente consulta el endpoint y sus respuestas declaradas, escribe un caso de prueba a partir del esquema validado y luego ejecuta todos los casos de ese endpoint:

Igual que el kernel de Lean, la especificación es el árbitro: cuando el backend se desvía, la ejecución falla y el agente te dice qué campo ha roto. Pon el mismo comando test-case run ... -r junit en CI para que se compruebe cada pull request; la guía de Apidog CLI para CI/CD muestra la configuración con GitHub Actions, y Apidog CLI en Claude Code cubre la parte del agente. Para la teoría de pruebas que hay detrás, consulta pruebas de contrato de API. El plan gratuito de Apidog admite hasta 4 usuarios.

¿Para qué se usa Lean 4? Lean 4 se usa para formalizar matemáticas (Mathlib, el proyecto del último teorema de Fermat), para verificar software y hardware, y como comprobador en la demostración automática de teoremas con IA. También es un lenguaje funcional de propósito general que compila a código nativo.

¿Claude ha demostrado la hipótesis de Riemann? Levent Alpöge afirma que encontró una demostración de la hipótesis de Riemann generalizada trabajando con Claude y la publicó como código Lean. Lean ha comprobado el código; los matemáticos siguen determinando qué demuestran esos 17 millones de líneas, algo que calculan que llevará semanas.

¿Lean 4 es gratis? Sí. Lean 4 y Mathlib son de código abierto, y el Lean FRO es una organización sin ánimo de lucro. Puedes ejecutarlo en local con elan o en el playground del navegador sin coste alguno.

¿Puede equivocarse un comprobador de demostraciones? En principio, sí, y por eso Lean mantiene pequeño el kernel de confianza y admite la reverificación independiente con herramientas como Comparator. El mayor riesgo práctico es un enunciado de teorema que no diga lo que querías decir.

¿Necesito saber matemáticas avanzadas para aprender Lean 4? No. Empieza con teoremas sencillos sobre números naturales y listas, o con Lean como lenguaje de programación. El proyecto tutorial de Mathlib y el playground están pensados para principiantes.

#9759. Qu’est-ce que Lean 4 ? Le vérificateur de preuves derrière la preuve de Riemann de Claude

Posted on Nov 23 • Originally published at apidog.com

Qu'est-ce que Lean 4 ? Lean 4 est un langage de programmation open source et un assistant de preuve qui vérifie pas à pas les preuves mathématiques et les propriétés des programmes, grâce à un petit noyau de confiance qui accepte ou rejette chaque inférence. C'est l'outil que le chercheur d'Anthropic Levent Alpöge a utilisé en novembre 2026 pour publier une preuve vérifiée par machine, élaborée avec Claude, qui selon lui résout l'hypothèse de Riemann généralisée.

Ce guide explique comment le vérificateur de preuves de Lean décide de ce qui est vrai, ce que l'affaire Riemann montre et ne montre pas, et comment lancer votre première preuve.

Lean 4 est un langage de programmation fonctionnel et un démonstrateur de théorèmes interactif. Vous énoncez un théorème sous forme de type, vous écrivez une preuve sous forme de programme de ce type, et le noyau de Lean vérifie chaque étape. Si le noyau l'accepte, la preuve est correcte au regard de la logique et des axiomes de Lean. Si une seule étape échoue, le fichier ne compile pas.

Quelques faits tirés de la page d'historique de la Lean FRO :

Lean réunit deux outils en un : un langage qui compile en code natif, et un assistant de preuve dont le système de types dépendants permet de démontrer que votre code respecte sa spécification pour toutes les entrées possibles, pas seulement pour celles que vous avez testées.

Le vendredi 20 novembre 2026, Levent Alpöge, membre du personnel technique d'Anthropic, a publié sur son site une note de quatre pages : « Je pense avoir découvert, en travaillant avec Claude, une preuve de l'hypothèse de Riemann. » Il n'a pas publié d'article scientifique classique. Il a livré son argumentation sous forme de code Lean, rapporte Al Jazeera, en écrivant que « Claude m'a largement dépassé sur la dernière ligne droite ».

Précisons bien le périmètre, car beaucoup de titres ne le font pas :

Pourquoi Lean est-il décisif ici ? Personne ne peut lire 17 millions de lignes. Cette affirmation mérite l'attention précisément parce qu'un petit programme, étudié de longue date, les a déjà toutes vérifiées.

Lean répartit le travail entre un front-end non fiable et un back-end de confiance. Toute l'intelligence se trouve dans le front-end. Tout ce en quoi vous devez avoir confiance réside dans le noyau, que le site de Lean décrit comme un « noyau de confiance minimal ».

C'est pourquoi une preuve écrite par une IA peut être digne de confiance : la plupart des tentatives sont fausses, et seuls les termes acceptés par le noyau survivent.

Deux échappatoires méritent votre attention. sorry permet de sauter une étape, et Lean signale chaque déclaration qui l'utilise. Les axiomes supplémentaires permettent de poser des hypothèses. La commande #print axioms liste tous les axiomes dont dépend un théorème : un relecteur voit ainsi en une ligne si quelque chose a été supposé.

Voici un fichier Lean 4 complet que vous pouvez coller dans le bac à sable Lean :

Les relecteurs d'un résultat majeur vérifient cela en premier : pas de sorry, pas d'axiome inattendu.

La démonstration automatique de théorèmes par IA fonctionne en boucle : le modèle propose, Lean répond, le modèle réessaie. Les erreurs et les objectifs ouverts renvoyés par Lean constituent le retour d'information ; le verdict du noyau est sans appel.

C'est le même schéma que celui de travaux antérieurs dont vous avez peut-être entendu parler. AlphaProof de Google DeepMind a atteint le niveau médaille d'argent aux IMO en juillet 2024 en s'appuyant sur Lean et Mathlib, et des modèles ouverts comme DeepSeek Prover V2 et DeepSeekMath-V2 s'entraînent sur Lean ou auto-vérifient leurs propres étapes.

C'est Mathlib qui permet de passer à l'échelle. Le site de Lean la décrit comme une bibliothèque communautaire de « plus d'un million de lignes de mathématiques formalisées », couvrant l'algèbre, l'analyse, la topologie et les probabilités. Une preuve sur les fonctions L ne part pas des axiomes de l'arithmétique ; elle s'appuie sur ce que Mathlib a déjà vérifié.

Les développeurs connaissent une version affaiblie de cette idée : les tests.

Une preuve peut être parfaite et démontrer pourtant autre chose que ce que vous vouliez : c'est pourquoi les mathématiciens vont passer des semaines à lire ce qu'énonce le code Lean d'Alpöge. Un test prouve moins, mais il coûte peu et s'exécute à chaque commit.

Pour une installation locale, suivez le guide d'installation officiel :

La leçon de Lean pour les équipes API est simple : écrivez le contrat noir sur blanc, puis laissez une machine vérifier chaque résultat par rapport à lui. Dans le travail sur les API, le contrat c'est votre spécification, et la vérification c'est la validation des réponses.

Apidog valide une réponse par rapport au schéma déclaré dans la spécification de votre endpoint : les champs manquants, les types erronés et les propriétés en trop apparaissent sans assertions écrites à la main. Apidog CLI permet à votre agent de codage d'exécuter ces vérifications à votre place, exactement comme Claude faisait tourner Lean en boucle. Vous écrivez un seul prompt ; l'agent lit la spécification, rédige des cas de test et les exécute.

Puis donnez un seul prompt à Claude Code, Codex ou Cursor :

L'agent consulte l'endpoint et les réponses qu'il déclare, rédige un cas de test à partir du schéma validé, puis exécute tous les cas de cet endpoint :

Comme le noyau de Lean, la spécification fait office d'arbitre : si le backend dérive, l'exécution échoue et l'agent vous indique quel champ a cassé. Placez la même commande test-case run ... -r junit dans votre CI pour que chaque pull request soit vérifiée ; le guide Apidog CLI pour la CI/CD montre la configuration GitHub Actions, et Apidog CLI dans Claude Code couvre le côté agent. Pour la théorie des tests qui sous-tend tout cela, voir le test de contrat d'API. La formule gratuite d'Apidog couvre jusqu'à 4 utilisateurs.

À quoi sert Lean 4 ? Lean 4 sert à formaliser les mathématiques (Mathlib, le projet du dernier théorème de Fermat), à vérifier des logiciels et du matériel, et de vérificateur dans la démonstration automatique de théorèmes par IA. C'est aussi un langage fonctionnel généraliste qui compile en code natif.

Claude a-t-il démontré l'hypothèse de Riemann ? Levent Alpöge affirme avoir trouvé, en travaillant avec Claude, une preuve de l'hypothèse de Riemann généralisée, et l'avoir publiée sous forme de code Lean. Lean a vérifié ce code ; les mathématiciens cherchent encore ce que montrent ces 17 millions de lignes, ce qui devrait leur prendre des semaines.

Lean 4 est-il gratuit ? Oui. Lean 4 et Mathlib sont open source, et la Lean FRO est une association à but non lucratif. Vous pouvez l'exécuter localement avec elan ou dans le bac à sable du navigateur, sans rien payer.

Un vérificateur de preuves peut-il se tromper ? En principe oui, c'est pourquoi Lean garde un noyau de confiance réduit et permet une revérification indépendante avec des outils comme Comparator. Le vrai risque, en pratique, c'est un énoncé de théorème qui ne dit pas ce que vous vouliez dire.

Faut-il connaître les mathématiques avancées pour apprendre Lean 4 ? Non. Commencez par des théorèmes simples sur les entiers naturels et les listes, ou abordez Lean comme un langage de programmation. Le projet de tutoriel de Mathlib et le bac à sable sont conçus pour les débutants.
