#9758. Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code.

To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. It's also available through our API.

We're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

#9757. How to Modernize Bank Without Taking Its Payment Systems Offline

Senior Solution Architect, Diebold Nixdorf. 16 years in secure payments, ATM/POS and digital banking. MSc AI candidate.

Senior Solution Architect, Diebold Nixdorf. 16 years in secure payments, ATM/POS and digital banking. MSc AI candidate.

Senior Solution Architect, Diebold Nixdorf. 16 years in secure payments, ATM/POS and digital banking. MSc AI candidate.

Every bank I have worked with has a system nobody wants to touch.

Sometimes it is a mainframe core banking platform written in COBOL. Sometimes it is a card switch that has been processing ISO 8583 messages reliably for twenty years. Sometimes it is a batch file job that runs at 2 a.m. and that exactly one engineer understands. These systems are old, but they are not broken. They move real money every second.

And yet the business wants mobile apps, open banking APIs, real-time payments and cloud analytics. The question is never "should we modernize?" The question is "how do we modernize without taking the ATM network offline on a Friday payday?"

After roughly sixteen years building ATM, POS and digital banking middleware for banks across the Middle East, Asia and Europe, here is what I have seen actually work.

The tempting plan is to replace the old core in one program. It rarely goes well. Large core replacements have a long public history of delays, outages and customers locked out of their accounts. The reasons repeat:

The alternative is incremental modernization. Less exciting, far more survivable.

Before writing new code, build an inventory of every point where systems talk to each other: protocols (ISO 8583, SWIFT MT/MX, ISO 20022, flat files, SOAP, proprietary TCP), message volumes, peak times, and who owns each interface.

In most banks this map reveals a "spaghetti" of point-to-point links. The ATM switch talks directly to the core. The mobile app calls a SOAP service that calls another SOAP service that writes to a shared database. Every new channel added another direct connection.

You cannot modernize what you have not mapped. You also cannot secure it.

The single most valuable move is introducing a governed integration layer between channels and back-end systems. This can be an API gateway plus a payment middleware or message broker, depending on the flow.

With the layer in place, use the strangler fig pattern: move one business flow at a time from legacy to new, while the rest keeps running untouched.

For each flow, run the new path in shadow mode first: send traffic to both systems, compare results, and only switch over when mismatches are near zero. Keep the routing switch reversible for weeks, not hours.

Integration layers are where security quietly degrades. Patterns I see repeatedly:

This matters well beyond one bank. In the United States, CISA identifies financial services as critical infrastructure, and regulators such as the FFIEC and OCC have repeatedly flagged third-party and legacy integration risk. As U.S. banks connect older cores to real-time rails like the Federal Reserve's FedNow Service and to ISO 20022 messaging, the integration layer becomes the front line of payment security.

During migration, two systems may each believe they own the truth. Automate reconciliation between legacy and new ledgers daily at minimum, and in near real time for payment flows. Every mismatch is either a migration bug or a hidden business rule you did not know about. Both are worth finding before customers do.

Teams celebrate when the new system goes live and forget to decommission the old path. Two systems running forever means double the attack surface and double the cost. For each migrated flow, define:

Legacy banking systems are not the enemy. They are proof that something worked for decades. Modernization succeeds when it respects that, puts a disciplined integration layer between old and new, moves one flow at a time, and treats security and reconciliation as part of the design.

The banks that get this right do not make headlines. Their customers simply never notice the migration happened. That is the goal.

Senior Solution Architect, Diebold Nixdorf. 16 years in secure payments, ATM/POS and digital banking. MSc AI candidate.

#9756. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features

Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.

To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.

When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows).

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab.

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts.

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. #9755. O que é Lean 4? O verificador de provas por trás da prova de Riemann de Claude

Posted on Nov 23 • Originally published at apidog.com

O que é o Lean 4? O Lean 4 é uma linguagem de programação de código aberto e um assistente de provas que verifica provas matemáticas e propriedades de programas passo a passo, com um pequeno kernel confiável que aceita ou rejeita cada inferência. É a ferramenta que o pesquisador da Anthropic Levent Alpöge usou em novembro de 2026 para publicar uma prova verificada por máquina, construída com o Claude, que, segundo ele, resolve a hipótese de Riemann generalizada.

Este guia explica como o verificador de provas do Lean decide o que é verdadeiro, o que a alegação sobre Riemann mostra — e o que não mostra — e como rodar sua primeira prova.

O Lean 4 é uma linguagem de programação funcional e um provador de teoremas interativo. Você enuncia um teorema como um tipo, escreve uma prova como um programa desse tipo, e o kernel do Lean verifica cada passo. Se o kernel aceitar, a prova está correta em relação à lógica e aos axiomas do Lean. Se algum passo falhar, o arquivo não compila.

Alguns fatos tirados da própria página de história do Lean FRO:

O Lean são duas ferramentas em uma: uma linguagem que compila para código nativo e um assistente de provas cujo sistema de tipos dependentes permite provar que o código atende à sua especificação para todas as entradas, não só para as que você testou.

Na sexta-feira, 20 de novembro de 2026, Levent Alpöge, membro da equipe técnica da Anthropic, publicou uma nota de quatro páginas em seu site: "Acredito ter, trabalhando com o Claude, descoberto uma prova da Hipótese de Riemann." Ele não publicou um artigo convencional. Divulgou o argumento como código Lean, noticiou a Al Jazeera, e escreveu que "o Claude me superou de longe perto da linha de chegada".

Entenda o escopo corretamente, porque muitas manchetes não o fazem:

Por que o Lean importa aqui? Ninguém consegue ler 17 milhões de linhas. A alegação merece atenção porque um programa pequeno e bem estudado já verificou cada uma delas.

O Lean divide o trabalho entre um front end não confiável e um back end confiável. Tudo o que é inteligente acontece no front end. Tudo o que você precisa confiar fica no kernel, que o site do Lean descreve como um "kernel confiável mínimo".

É por isso que dá para confiar em uma prova escrita por IA: a maioria das tentativas está errada, e só sobrevivem os termos que o kernel aceita.

Duas válvulas de escape importam. O sorry permite pular um passo, e o Lean sinaliza toda declaração que o usa. Axiomas extras permitem assumir coisas. O comando #print axioms lista todos os axiomas dos quais um teorema depende, então um revisor vê em uma única linha se algo foi assumido.

Aqui está um arquivo Lean 4 completo para colar no playground do Lean:

Quem revisa um resultado importante verifica isto primeiro: nenhum sorry, nenhum axioma inesperado.

A prova de teoremas com IA funciona em loop. O modelo propõe, o Lean responde, o modelo tenta de novo. Os erros e objetivos em aberto do Lean são o feedback; o veredito do kernel é definitivo.

É o mesmo padrão por trás de trabalhos anteriores sobre os quais você talvez tenha lido. O AlphaProof, do Google DeepMind, alcançou desempenho de medalha de prata na IMO em julho de 2024 usando Lean e a Mathlib, e modelos abertos como o DeepSeek Prover V2 e o DeepSeekMath-V2 treinam com base no Lean ou verificam seus próprios passos.

A Mathlib é o motivo pelo qual isso escala. O site do Lean a descreve como uma biblioteca da comunidade com "mais de um milhão de linhas de matemática formalizada", abrangendo álgebra, análise, topologia e probabilidade. Uma prova sobre funções L não começa dos axiomas da aritmética; ela se apoia no que a Mathlib já verificou.

Desenvolvedores conhecem uma versão mais fraca dessa ideia: os testes.

Uma prova pode ser perfeita e ainda assim provar o enunciado errado, e é por isso que os matemáticos vão passar semanas lendo o que o código Lean de Alpöge enuncia. Um teste prova menos, mas é barato e roda a cada commit.

Para uma instalação local, siga o guia oficial de instalação manual:

A lição do Lean para times de API é simples: escreva o contrato e deixe uma máquina verificar cada resultado contra ele. No trabalho com APIs, o contrato é a sua especificação, e a verificação é a validação de resposta.

O Apidog valida uma resposta contra o schema que a especificação do seu endpoint declara, então campos ausentes, tipos errados e propriedades extras aparecem sem asserções escritas à mão. O Apidog CLI permite que seu agente de código rode essas verificações para você, do mesmo jeito que o Claude rodava o Lean em loop. Você escreve um prompt; o agente lê a especificação, escreve os casos de teste e os executa.

Depois, dê um prompt ao Claude Code, ao Codex ou ao Cursor:

O agente consulta o endpoint e as respostas declaradas, escreve um caso de teste a partir do schema validado e então roda todos os casos do endpoint:

Assim como o kernel do Lean, a especificação é o árbitro: quando o backend se desvia, a execução falha e o agente informa qual campo quebrou. Coloque o mesmo comando test-case run ... -r junit no CI para que todo pull request seja verificado; o guia de CI/CD do Apidog CLI mostra a configuração no GitHub Actions, e Apidog CLI no Claude Code cobre o lado do agente. Para a teoria de testes por trás disso, veja teste de contrato de API. O plano Free do Apidog atende até 4 usuários.

Para que serve o Lean 4? O Lean 4 é usado para formalizar matemática (Mathlib, o projeto do Último Teorema de Fermat), para verificar software e hardware e como verificador na prova de teoremas com IA. Também é uma linguagem funcional de uso geral que compila para código nativo.

O Claude provou a hipótese de Riemann? Levent Alpöge afirma ter encontrado, trabalhando com o Claude, uma prova da hipótese de Riemann generalizada, e a divulgou como código Lean. O Lean verificou o código; os matemáticos ainda estão descobrindo o que as 17 milhões de linhas mostram, algo que deve levar semanas.

O Lean 4 é gratuito? Sim. O Lean 4 e a Mathlib são de código aberto, e o Lean FRO é uma organização sem fins lucrativos. Você pode rodá-lo localmente com o elan ou no playground do navegador, sem custo.

Um verificador de provas pode errar? Em princípio, sim, e é por isso que o Lean mantém o kernel confiável pequeno e oferece suporte à reverificação independente com ferramentas como o Comparator. O risco prático maior é um enunciado de teorema que não diz o que você queria dizer.

Preciso saber matemática avançada para aprender Lean 4? Não. Comece com teoremas simples sobre números naturais e listas, ou com o Lean como linguagem de programação. O projeto de tutorial da Mathlib e o playground foram feitos para iniciantes.

#9754. 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:

Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:

The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:

Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

#9753. Seven secondhand machines run most of our infrastructure. Here is what broke.

Mouve's production runs on six small virtual machines in Helsinki. Everything else runs in our office in Tallinn, on seven secondhand machines: two HP Z440 workstations, a dual-Xeon workstation board with three GPUs, a Dell PowerEdge T40 tower, a Dell Latitude laptop with the lid closed, and two small desktop PCs.

The office end of Mouve: the two HP Z440s on the bottom shelf, the Dell T40 and a UPS above them, the rackmount cases higher up, and the small PCs in the mesh cabinet on the right.

Together they are 160 threads, 369 GB of RAM and about 10 TB of disk. They run our CI, the dev environment, the agents that write much of our code, the monitoring, the backups and the GPU work. This post is about the hardware: why I chose it, how I reach it when it hangs, and the things that broke. It follows two posts about our costs, what our CI would cost on hosted runners and what our CI fixes measured, which say the hardware is cheap to run. That is true, and it leaves out how much work goes into making it dependable. I leave out purchase prices here; the comparison I care about is running cost.

The lease includes electricity. I confirmed that on 2026-09-04, and it changes the usual homelab advice. The standard argument against a dual-socket Xeon is that it burns its purchase price in power. Here a 150 W box costs us the same to run as a 15 W one.

So I judge hardware on capacity, heat and noise. The filter for the workstations was a platform with registered ECC memory that is easy to find used (LGA2011-3 sockets, the C610 family of chipsets). A rack server with small fast fans is out because people sit in the office.

That is a real advantage, and it has limits. Over the last 30 days the whole cluster averaged 27 cores and 169 GB, and the hourly 95th percentile was 105 cores. The machines are sized for the peaks, which come from CI and agents. On the evening of 2026-11-20, kubectl top nodes showed about 13.6 cores and 127 GiB in use across all seven. Idle capacity costs us nothing, and I won't pretend it is a feature.

The three control planes are deliberately boring. I learned why on 2026-05-20.

Before the current cluster, one control-plane node had a consumer 2.5-inch SATA SSD. SMART said it was healthy. It still made the node flip between Ready and NotReady about 16 times in 100 minutes.

The cause was fsync. etcd writes its log and waits for the disk to confirm it. A consumer drive without power-loss protection confirms slowly, and ours took 200 to 500 ms per write when it should take under 10. containerd then blocked on the same disk, the kubelet's calls to it timed out, and the node was marked down. From outside it looked like a network flap.

The rule I took from it is simple: etcd and anything that syncs goes on a drive with power-loss protection. The control planes now boot from Intel data-centre SATA SSDs. One also has a consumer NVMe that arrived with the box. I gave it one job, staged etcd snapshots, because a torn snapshot can be detected and retaken and a torn etcd log cannot.

The same lesson came back in a different place. On 2026-08-30 I measured one Z440 that felt slow in ways that looked like four different problems. CI containers stuck for minutes unpacking, the kubelet's health check stalled, kubectl exec hung, and storage replicas faulted.

All of it traced to one cheap SATA SSD with no DRAM cache that held the OS partition, container layers and every emptyDir. It was 92 to 99% busy at 13 MB/s of writes while the 2 TB NVMe next to it sat at 13%. I moved /var to the NVMe in September, and the 95th-percentile write latency on that path went from 193 ms to 17 ms.

Then on 2026-11-16 I gave the other Z440 a 250 GB consumer SATA SSD (a used drive with 30,548 power-on hours) as its CI cache. On a busy night the runners wrote the whole drive in about 20 to 25 minutes and deleted about as much. Write throughput fell from over 200 MB/s to about 55 MB/s, with latency up from 4 ms to 15 to 25 ms.

The weekly TRIM had run, and latency was best right after it, then tripled within the hour. My guess is that without regular TRIM the drive had almost no clean blocks to work with. It fits the data, but I haven't proved it. I now trim every 15 minutes with a small CronJob, and I took that node out of the CI pools until it has a share it can drain.

Bytes were not the only thing that ran out on those CI cache disks. Inodes did too, and they did it first.

On 2026-10-23 every job on the self-hosted pools started failing with No space left on device, while df -h showed 78 to 87% used. df -i showed 99%. Each CI working tree is only about 300 MB, but it is 20,000 to 30,000 inodes. Dozens of agent pull requests produced 25 to 95 finished runner pods a minute, and the reclaimer that deletes old trees managed 12 to 20 per minute. The inode count went from 0.5% to 99.9% used in two hours.

Nothing paged, because our alerts read bytes only and the stock inode alert waits two hours.

On 2026-11-16 the same thing happened faster on the smaller SSD. It has about 15 million inodes against 39 million on the NVMe, and it went from 73% free to 80,000 inodes free in an hour. I made the reclaimer speed up as the disk fills, shortened the alert windows, and recorded the fix for the real cause: format the disk with more inodes. Measured on that night, our cache used 13 to 14 KB per inode, so ext4's default of one inode per 16 KiB runs out first.

The class of failure is that a small cache outruns settings that were tuned for a big one. The rule I wrote down: the inflow a node is given must stay below the rate its cache disk can drain.

At 19:24 UTC on 2026-10-02 the second Z440 stopped. Not a reboot: a freeze. The switch port stayed up at gigabit but received nothing, so neither the host nor its management engine was sending. The cluster marked it NotReady, and it stayed down until 23:00.

The cause, read off the BIOS screen after the recovery boot, was a fatal machine check: an uncorrectable memory read error on the first CPU's memory controller, DIMM 1 or 2. The error came two minutes into a burst of heavy CPU work that took the processor package from 61 to 80 °C, on a board with no memory fan fitted. The BIOS prints "Memory configuration requires a Memory fan and this fan is not detected" on every boot, and halts until someone presses Enter.

On 2026-10-25 a full 32 GB memtester pass came back clean, with no corrected or uncorrected errors on any of the four DIMMs after 4 hours 40 minutes at about 40 °C. I put the original error down to heat, because the case fans were not running at the time, and I did not replace the DIMM. I haven't proved that, and I alert on memory errors now.

The more useful lesson was the 3.5 hours. Postgres had a healthy second replica on the other Z440, but every dev workload carried a hostname pin from an earlier move, so nothing could start anywhere else. I replaced the pins with a role label and added a CI guard that fails on any single-node pin. A failover drill the next morning moved dev's database to the other node with about 45 seconds of downtime. The API image still took 9 minutes 11 seconds to pull there, because that node had never run that tag.

Both Z440s have Intel AMT, the management engine that sits below the operating system. It gives us remote power control with the machine fully off, and a serial console over the network. I use plain HTTP calls to it, no vendor tools. The first Z440's AMT was dark when we last checked on 2026-10-03, and we have not verified it since.

Neither Z440 has a memory fan fitted, so every cold boot still needs someone, or an agent on the serial line, to press Enter. I have a part number for a shroud with a fan. I have not fitted one.

For about six weeks the office control plane had two etcd members and no fault tolerance. One of the three machines, a small PC, had died on 2026-09-01 without a cause I could find, and no POST output reached us remotely. On 2026-10-12 I moved its boot SSD into the Dell T40, and the node came back with its identity, rejoined as the same etcd member and caught up from a snapshot.

Before that, on 2026-10-01, the control plane started losing its leader about 39 times an hour. The API server's 99th-percentile latency went from 0.046 s to 2 to 7 s. Watches got HTTP 429s. The controller manager restarted 63 times a day per control plane, and CI runner controllers crash-looped, so CI queued.

I suspected the disks first, because of the earlier incident. They were fine: Intel data-centre SSDs, 0.18 ms average write, no slow step in any trace.

The cause was the network. Our nodes talk over a mesh VPN, and our CNI, Cilium, carries its VXLAN overlay on top of that mesh. The VPN daemon advertises every local address as a possible endpoint, including the CNI's own. It sent some of its own encrypted packets into the overlay, which wrapped them and sent them back into the VPN. The loop overflowed the tunnel interface's queue and dropped 1,000 to 13,000 packets a second in bursts. The etcd peer link uses the same interface. With two voters the leader needs the other to answer within one second, and each burst missed that.

The fix was four routing rules on every node that make the VPN daemon's own packets unreachable for the pod and service ranges. A DaemonSet asserts them every 30 seconds, so a reboot cannot lose them. After they went in at 09:14 UTC on 2026-10-03: zero elections, zero drops. I never found what started it on 2026-10-01. The rules make the trigger irrelevant.

The existing alert described the symptom, slow etcd requests, and said nothing about why. I added alerts for tunnel packet drops, watch-cache re-initialisation and control-plane restarts, each backtested against the history.

I started Kubernetes on k3s in March 2026. At the end of May I planned the move to Talos: reinstall the same physical hardware, one node at a time.

Talos has no shell and everything goes through an API. The price is that tasks you would do over ssh become small pods, such as the guard pod we use to check routing rules. Today five of the seven nodes run Talos. The two GPU machines still run Ubuntu. The one with the RTX 3060 stays on Ubuntu because iterating on NVIDIA drivers is faster on a stock OS than through Talos system extensions, where every driver bump means rebuilding the image and reflashing the node.

The best thing it bought us was the 2026-10-12 hardware swap above: the node's identity lived on its boot disk, so a different machine came up as the same etcd member.

I ended up with three kinds of storage, and the rule is what the data needs when it is lost.

That last choice has a cost I accepted knowingly. The backups and the things they protect now share a building. A fire, a theft, or a bad write that the mirror copies would take both. The cheap fix is a copy on another site, and I have not done it.

None of this is glamorous. All of Mouve's infrastructure costs about EUR 85 a month to run, of which about EUR 74 is the Hetzner VMs for production, and the office electricity is in the rent. What the office cluster costs me is attention: the nights when a freeze, a full table or a loop teaches me something a hosted service would have hidden.

Mouve is a fitness and nutrition app from Estonia: track your training, scan your food, and step into a world of fitness built around games and competition. Built in public by one founder and a fleet of AI agents.

#9751. Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases

Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them

Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:

Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in four ways:

-Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

-Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

-Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:

Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

Explore the models on Confluent to see how time-series intelligence can support real-time decisions.

#9750. WARN Act and Your On-Call Pay — What Happens to Standby Pay After a Layoff Notice

Posted on Nov 23 • Originally published at layoffatlas.com

A WARN notice tells you your job is ending in at least 60 days. If part of your pay comes from being on call — nights, weekends, holidays, waiting for the phone to ring — the notice raises a practical question: do you keep getting that standby pay, and for how long?

The short answer: on-call pay is tied to the job, not to the notice. It usually continues while you are still employed and on the rotation, and stops on the effective date. The details matter, because on-call arrangements vary.

Fresh from Layoff Atlas: 749 WARN notices covering 61,461 reported workers in the current 90-day window, updated November 22, 2026. California leads with 23,941 workers, and the heaviest upcoming effective week is December 28, with 10,412. These are reported plans, not confirmed job losses.

On-call pay compensates you for being available to work outside scheduled hours. It is common in health care, IT support, utilities, and maintenance — anywhere something can break at 2 a.m.

Some employers pay a flat standby rate for every hour on call. Others pay only when you are called in, sometimes at overtime rates.

Federal law draws its own line. Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, on-call time counts as hours worked — and must be paid — when you are so restricted you cannot use the time for your own purposes. Waiting at the plant, or required to respond within minutes, usually counts. Carrying a pager at home, free to go about your life, usually does not.

The WARN Act is a notice law, not a pay law. It requires covered employers — generally those with 100 or more full-time workers — to give 60 days' written notice before a mass layoff or plant closure. It does not set pay rates, require severance, or create any special right to on-call premiums.

Your on-call pay is governed by employer policy, your contract, the FLSA, and state wage laws. WARN's contribution is the notice period: 60 days of continued employment under the same pay rules as before.

While you are still employed, on-call pay works the way it always did. On the rotation and available, the standby premium is owed. Called in, the call-out pay is owed. Nothing in a WARN notice suspends those rules.

Two things can change the picture. First, the employer may shrink the rotation. As operations wind down, the employer may take you off the on-call list. That is usually lawful — on-call pay is pay for a duty, and when the duty goes away, the premium goes with it. What the employer generally cannot do is keep you on call and stop paying for it.

Second, watch for schedule cuts. If your employer drops your on-call shifts during the notice period, keep records of what you worked — defective-notice back-pay claims are measured by the pay you would have received.

Some states add their own rules: California and New York have reporting-time and call-in pay rules that can apply when a shift is cut short or cancelled. A WARN notice does not override them.

On the effective date, employment ends, and on-call pay ends with it. There is no standby duty after your last day, and no standby premium to go with it. Unlike health insurance, which can continue under COBRA, on-call pay has no continuation right.

If a standby stipend was paid in advance, it may stop on your last day. If it was paid in arrears for time already served, the unpaid portion is wages owed and should appear on your final paycheck under your state's wage-payment law.

Check severance, too: it is usually based on base pay or length of service, and on-call premiums are often excluded. If on-call pay was a large share of your income, ask HR in writing whether it counts — before you sign a release.

Start with the paper trail: on-call schedules, call logs, and pay stubs showing the standby rate. Note the dates and hours of every call-in. That record is what turns a disagreement into a claim.

Ask HR, in writing, whether on-call rotations continue through the notice period and how call-out pay will be handled on your final check.

If pay for time already served is missing from your final check, the remedy runs through wage law, not WARN: a complaint with the U.S. Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division or your state labor agency. On-call earnings also count as wages for unemployment insurance.

On-call pay is one of the quieter pieces of a layoff, and that is exactly why it gets missed. The notice period is 60 days of continued employment, and the standby premium is still pay for work during those 60 days — as long as you are still the one standing by.

#9749. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.
