#9740. Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:

Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:

We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:

Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:

858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

This example shows how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:

The figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which showed that 0.1 worked best).

We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

Each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:

Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

The number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

We concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each update below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:

The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own update. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):

"Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi automatically applies context compaction, while OpenCode and Hermes don't, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

All three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

We appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

This question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

This phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

However this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

Throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

We also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

Train open models with RL inside real agent harnesses

#9739. Lean 4 Nedir? Claude Riemann Kanıtının Arkasındaki İspat Denetleyicisi

Posted on Nov 23 • Originally published at apidog.com

Lean 4 nedir? Lean 4, matematiksel ispatları ve program özelliklerini adım adım denetleyen, her çıkarımı kabul eden ya da reddeden küçük ve güvenilir bir çekirdeğe sahip açık kaynaklı bir programlama dili ve ispat asistanıdır. Anthropic araştırmacısı Levent Alpöge'nin Kasım 2026'da, Claude ile birlikte geliştirerek yayımladığı ve genelleştirilmiş Riemann hipotezini çözdüğünü söylediği makine tarafından denetlenmiş ispatı duyurduğu araç da budur.

Bu rehber, Lean'in ispat denetleyicisinin neyin doğru olduğuna nasıl karar verdiğini, Riemann iddiasının neyi gösterip neyi göstermediğini ve ilk ispatınızı nasıl çalıştıracağınızı açıklar.

Lean 4, fonksiyonel bir programlama dili ve etkileşimli bir teorem ispatlayıcıdır. Bir teoremi bir tip olarak ifade edersiniz, o tipte bir program yazarak ispatı oluşturursunuz ve Lean'in çekirdeği her adımı denetler. Çekirdek ispatı kabul ederse, ispat Lean'in mantığına ve aksiyomlarına göre doğrudur. Herhangi bir adım başarısız olursa dosya derlenmez.

Lean FRO'nun kendi tarihçe sayfasından birkaç bilgi:

Lean, tek bir araçta iki ayrı aracı birleştirir: yerel koda derlenen bir dil ve bağımlı tip sistemine sahip bir ispat asistanı. Bu tip sistemi, kodunuzun spesifikasyonu yalnızca test ettiğiniz girdiler için değil, her olası girdi için karşıladığını kanıtlamanıza olanak tanır.

20 Kasım 2026 Cuma günü, Anthropic teknik ekibinden Levent Alpöge kendi web sitesinde dört sayfalık bir not yayımladı: "Claude ile birlikte çalışarak Riemann Hipotezi'nin bir ispatını keşfettiğime inanıyorum." Geleneksel bir makale yayımlamadı. Al Jazeera'nın haberine göre ispatı Lean kodu olarak yayımladı ve "bitiş çizgisine yaklaşırken Claude beni çok geride bıraktı" diye yazdı.

Kapsamı doğru anlamak önemli, çünkü pek çok manşet bunu yapmıyor:

Lean burada neden önemli? Kimse 17 milyon satırı okuyamaz. İddia dikkate değer, çünkü küçük ve iyi incelenmiş bir program bu satırların her birini zaten denetlemiş durumda.

Lean, işi güvenilmeyen bir ön uç ve güvenilen bir arka uç olarak ikiye ayırır. Akıllıca olan her şey ön uçta gerçekleşir. Güvenmeniz gereken her şey ise çekirdekte bulunur; Lean'in sitesi bunu "asgari güvenilir çekirdek" olarak tanımlar.

Yapay zekâ tarafından yazılmış bir ispata neden güvenilebileceği işte burada: denemelerin çoğu yanlıştır ve yalnızca çekirdeğin kabul ettiği terimler hayatta kalır.

İki kaçış noktası önemli. sorry bir adımı atlamanıza izin verir ve Lean bunu kullanan her bildirimi işaretler. Ekstra aksiyomlar bir şeyleri varsaymanıza olanak tanır. #print axioms komutu bir teoremin bağlı olduğu her aksiyomu listeler; böylece bir inceleyici tek satırda herhangi bir varsayımda bulunulup bulunulmadığını görebilir.

İşte Lean playground'a yapıştırabileceğiniz eksiksiz bir Lean 4 dosyası:

Büyük bir sonucun inceleyicileri önce buna bakar: sorry yok, beklenmedik aksiyom yok.

Yapay zekâ ile teorem ispatı bir döngü halinde işler. Model önerir, Lean yanıtlar, model yeniden dener. Lean'in hataları ve açık hedefleri geri bildirim işlevi görür; çekirdeğin kararı ise kesindir.

Bu, daha önce hakkında okumuş olabileceğiniz çalışmaların ardındaki aynı desendir. Google DeepMind'ın AlphaProof'u Temmuz 2024'te Lean ve Mathlib kullanarak IMO gümüş madalya performansına ulaştı; DeepSeek Prover V2 ve DeepSeekMath-V2 gibi açık modeller de Lean'e karşı eğitiliyor ya da kendi adımlarını kendileri doğruluyor.

Bu ölçeğin arkasındaki neden Mathlib. Lean'in sitesi Mathlib'i cebir, analiz, topoloji ve olasılığı kapsayan "bir milyon satırı aşkın formalize edilmiş matematik" içeren bir topluluk kütüphanesi olarak tanımlıyor. L-fonksiyonları hakkındaki bir ispat, aritmetiğin aksiyomlarından başlamaz; Mathlib'in halihazırda doğruladığı şeylerin üzerine inşa edilir.

Geliştiriciler bu fikrin daha zayıf bir versiyonunu bilir: testler.

Bir ispat kusursuz olup yine de yanlış ifadeyi ispatlayabilir; matematikçilerin haftalar boyunca Alpöge'nin Lean kodunun ne ifade ettiğini okumaya ayıracak olmasının nedeni de budur. Bir test daha azını ispatlar, ama ucuzdur ve her commit'te çalışır.

Yerel bir kurulum için resmi manuel kurulum kılavuzunu izleyin:

Lean'in API ekiplerine verdiği ders basittir: sözleşmeyi yazın, sonra her sonucu buna göre bir makinenin denetlemesini sağlayın. API çalışmalarında sözleşme, spesifikasyonunuzdur; denetim ise yanıt doğrulamasıdır.

Apidog, bir yanıtı uç nokta spesifikasyonunuzun bildirdiği şemaya göre doğrular; böylece eksik alanlar, yanlış tipler ve fazladan özellikler elle yazılmış doğrulama ifadelerine gerek kalmadan ortaya çıkar. Apidog CLI, kodlama ajanınızın bu denetimleri sizin için çalıştırmasını sağlar; tıpkı Claude'un Lean'i bir döngü içinde çalıştırması gibi. Siz tek bir istem yazarsınız; ajan spesifikasyonu okur, test senaryoları yazar ve bunları çalıştırır.

Ardından Claude Code, Codex veya Cursor'a tek bir istem verin:

Ajan uç noktayı ve bildirilen yanıtlarını bulur, doğrulanmış şemadan bir test senaryosu yazar ve ardından uç noktadaki her senaryoyu çalıştırır:

Lean'in çekirdeği gibi spesifikasyon da hakemdir: backend kaydığında çalıştırma başarısız olur ve ajan hangi alanın bozulduğunu size söyler. Aynı test-case run ... -r junit komutunu CI'a ekleyin ki her pull request denetlensin; Apidog CLI CI/CD rehberi GitHub Actions kurulumunu gösterir, Apidog CLI in Claude Code ise ajan tarafını ele alır. Bunun arkasındaki test teorisi için API sözleşme testlerine bakın. Apidog'un Ücretsiz planı 4 kullanıcıya kadar destekler.

Lean 4 ne için kullanılır? Lean 4, matematiği formalize etmek (Mathlib, Fermat'ın Son Teoremi projesi), yazılım ve donanımı doğrulamak ve yapay zekâ ile teorem ispatında denetleyici olarak kullanılır. Ayrıca yerel koda derlenen genel amaçlı bir fonksiyonel dildir.

Claude Riemann hipotezini ispatladı mı? Levent Alpöge, Claude ile çalışarak genelleştirilmiş Riemann hipotezinin bir ispatını bulduğunu ve bunu Lean kodu olarak yayımladığını söylüyor. Lean kodu denetledi; matematikçiler hâlâ 17 milyon satırın neyi gösterdiğini çözmeye çalışıyor ve bunun haftalar almasını bekliyorlar.

Lean 4 ücretsiz mi? Evet. Lean 4 ve Mathlib açık kaynaklıdır ve Lean FRO kâr amacı gütmeyen bir kuruluştur. Lean'i elan ile yerel olarak veya tarayıcıdaki playground'da ücretsiz çalıştırabilirsiniz.

Bir ispat denetleyicisi yanlış olabilir mi? İlke olarak evet; Lean'in güvenilir çekirdeği küçük tutup Comparator gibi araçlarla bağımsız yeniden denetimi desteklemesinin nedeni budur. Pratikteki asıl büyük risk, kastettiğiniz şeyi ifade etmeyen bir teorem ifadesidir.

Lean 4 öğrenmek için ileri düzey matematik bilmem gerekiyor mu? Hayır. Doğal sayılar ve listeler hakkındaki basit teoremlerle ya da Lean'i bir programlama dili olarak öğrenmeye başlayın. Mathlib'in öğretici projesi ve playground yeni başlayanlar için tasarlanmıştır.

#9738. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing.

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

Sounds like you're biased for Grammarly. Not really that informative if you're already leaning towards one to begin with. Still, it was an interesting read. Tell me, do you use Grammarly with your day-to-day writing/blogging?

I use the paid versions of both Grammarly and Pro Writing Aid. Both of them have issues:- Grammarly IS more focused on nonfiction than fiction. If you're writing fiction, you may find Grammarly's insistence on "Conciseness" annoying. They seem to want to take the soul out of your writing, which is fine for a corporate report or technical manual, but not for your Great American Novel.- Grammarly pushes features on users that are not ready for prime time. It doesn't matter that you never agreed to be a beta tester for them; you get to do it anyway.- Pro Writing Aid actually counts the occurrences of words in your document and tells you when a word has been overused compared to published literature. Grammarly, on the other hand, seems hell-bent to remove certain words that it has deemed overused from the language, whether or not they're actually overused in your document.- Grammarly's Clarity function is simply horrible. It mangles sentences and changes their meaning. Sometimes the result of its suggestion is unintelligible garbage.- Grammarly allows you to turn off some checks, but not all of them. Unfortunately, the ones you cannot turn off are some of the most irritating (such as that horrible "Clarity"). On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). The app insists on rules of grammar and spelling that are outright wrong, per Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and modern usage as shown by Google Books Ngram. At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

#9737. Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

We ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

In addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

To set the number of loops in the research checkpoint, you can modify the loop_num_passes in text_config as follows. The example below uses two loops.

For an image prompt, replace messages in either example with the list below and infer as usual.

Pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

Available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

In this example we ask our model about the current temperature at a given location. With the prompt, we also provide the tool (get_current_temperature) to do it. The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.

If you want to know more about tool calling, we recommend going to our official docs.

Llama App lets you easily run and manage local language models on macOS (from the menu bar) or Windows (system tray). It’s built on llama.cpp, and by the same team. The app also provides a local OpenAI-compatible API for easy integration with coding agents, editors, and scripts.

For the Inkling 2 Mini release we provide GGUF 4-bit (IQ4_NL) and 8-bit (Q8_0) quants for both models.

If you’re on Linux or you want to serve the model from the CLI, you can run the following command for the fixed-loop model:

To run the variable-loop model, you can run

To load the 8-bit weights, change the suffix to :Q8_0.

Here we ask the 4-bit model to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists. Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic.

Inkling 2 Mini comes with Day 0 support inside SGLang. You can install the latest version of SGLang and execute the following to get the server up and running. One prerequisite to take care of is to run it on SM103.

After the server is up you should be able to request the APIs like so

One can also enable multimodality by setting --enable-multimodal.

SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.

We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.

We upstreamed MLX support to the mlx-lm project, including multimodal image and text inputs, and shared quants through the mlx-community organization.

MLX inference works with the original checkpoint too. In this case, the native nvfp4 + mxfp8 quantization scheme is used without reconversion: you get the original quality the authors intended.

We have given Inkling 2 Mini a shot in many fun tasks, check them out in this section.

The same prompt produced two sunset flythroughs over procedural mountains and reflective water, each rendered with a single WebGL fragment shader.

Build the most impressive original real-time scene you can: a slow, cinematic camera flight over procedural mountains, through volumetric clouds and low over water with reflections, all lit by a sunset. Deliver it as a single self-contained index.html in the current directory that renders everything in one full-screen WebGL fragment shader, purely from code (no textures, images, fonts, libraries, external files or network requests of any kind). It must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080, aiming for 60 fps on a desktop GPU, with an automatic resolution-scale fallback that lowers the internal render resolution when the frame rate drops, and the flight must keep going indefinitely without glitches. To check your work, run node shot.cjs index.html shot.png 6 (the third argument is how many seconds to wait; a comma list such as 3,12,25 saves one screenshot per time, and an optional fourth argument sets the size, default 1280x720): it renders the page in headless Chrome, saves the screenshot(s), and prints the WebGL renderer, a rough frame rate and any console errors; then look at the images. The headless renderer on this machine may be software-only, so its frame rate can be far below what a real desktop GPU achieves and is not the target. Decide for yourself when the result is finished, then reply with a short description of what you built.

Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night (1889)

We gave Inkling 2 Mini a reference image of Van Gogh’s painting and a screenshot helper in the Pi coding harness. Inkling wrote a self-contained HTML page with a single WebGL2 fragment shader. The shader draws the scene from code without loading the reference image or any other assets. It uses time to animate the swirling sky, the glow of the stars, the swaying cypress, and the flicker of the village windows.

Inkling rendered and reviewed its work over 24 rounds of screenshot checks. We recorded the final animation frame by frame at 1080p and 60 fps on an Apple M4 Max.

In this folder, starry-night.jpg is Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889, public domain). Recreate it as a living painting: a single self-contained index.html (all code inline, no external files, libraries or network requests) that fills the browser window and runs smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Everything must be generated procedurally in code, for example with WebGL shaders; the page must not load, embed or sample starry-night.jpg or any other image. Stay faithful to the painting's composition and palette (the great spiral and swirling currents of the sky, the haloed stars, the glowing crescent moon, the dark flame-like cypress on the left, the rolling hills, and the village with its church spire), rendered in Van Gogh's thick, directional brushstrokes, and bring it to life: the sky's swirls flow, the stars and moon pulse with light, the cypress sways, and the village windows glow and flicker. Aim for the most impressive result you can make. A helper is provided: run node shot.js --help to see how to screenshot index.html at several moments; look at the screenshots next to the reference and keep improving until you are satisfied, then reply with a short summary of what you made.

We gave Inkling 2 Mini a photo of a hand-drawn Trip Split wireframe and a one-paragraph prompt in the Pi coding harness. Inkling used the sketch’s labels, sample expenses, and handwritten notes to build the expense list, add-expense form, and balances view in a single HTML file with vanilla CSS and JavaScript. The app updates totals and balances when expenses change, suggests payments to settle the trip, and saves data in the browser’s localStorage so it survives a reload.

We ran three independent Inkling attempts and used Playwright to click through each build, checking screenshots where visual judgment was needed. The first attempt, shown here, passed all 13 checks. Adding the sketch’s $90 dinner raised the total from $405 to $495 and recalculated what each person owed.

The photo sketch.jpg in this folder is a product designer's hand-drawn wireframe of a small app. Build that app for real, as the most impressive, original, production-quality version you can make: a single self-contained index.html in this folder using vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript only (no frameworks, CDNs, external files or network requests; localStorage is fine), which must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Treat everything on the paper as the spec: every screen, label, button and number, the example data, and each red note describe behaviour that must actually work, while the visual design, typography and motion are yours to make beautiful. Look at the sketch carefully with your vision, and use your vision again to check your own work: node shot.cjs --help explains a provided helper that screenshots index.html in headless Chrome at any window size after clicks or other JavaScript steps (Playwright is also installed if you prefer your own scripts), and you can look at any screenshot with the read tool. Click through every feature, compare each screen against the sketch, and keep improving until you are fully satisfied; then reply with a short summary of what you built.

We ask the 4-bit GGUF quantized Inkling 2 Mini (IQ4_NL) to make a website to a SaaS called plant therapy where plants get matched to licensed therapists.

Model is quite autonomous, it has made its own SVGs for the visuals on the website, and even built the matching logic, all from a short prompt: "Can you make a website for my saas called plant therapy where I match house plants with licensed therapists so plants don’t die, return single HTML”.

We have paired Inkling 2 Mini with Pi coding agent to build itself into a browser agent using Helium, Chromium and Hugging Face Sandboxes. We provide the traces and the final file (that can be used as a browser agent) in this bucket.

We are very glad to partner with Thinking Machines Lab to ship Inkling 2 Mini, a performant mid-sized model for local setups. Give this model a try and let us know what you think in comments!

Thank you for this article. It helped me in creating this hands-on video on this model https://youtu.be/BrN8dKfTU7M?si=8Cqg4igsdMY9OSJc

#9736. Lean 4 คืออะไร? ตัวตรวจสอบการพิสูจน์ที่อยู่เบื้องหลังการพิสูจน์ข้อคาดการณ์รีมันน์โดย Claude

Posted on Nov 23 • Originally published at apidog.com

Lean 4 คืออะไร? Lean 4 เป็นภาษาโปรแกรมและตัวช่วยพิสูจน์ (proof assistant) แบบโอเพนซอร์ส ที่ตรวจสอบข้อพิสูจน์ทางคณิตศาสตร์และคุณสมบัติของโปรแกรมทีละขั้นตอน ด้วย kernel ขนาดเล็กที่เชื่อถือได้ ซึ่งจะตอบรับหรือปฏิเสธทุกการอนุมาน เป็นเครื่องมือที่ Levent Alpöge นักวิจัยของ Anthropic ใช้ในเดือนพฤศจิกายน 2026 เพื่อเผยแพร่ข้อพิสูจน์ที่ผ่านการตรวจด้วยเครื่อง ซึ่งสร้างขึ้นด้วย Claude และเขาอ้างว่าพิสูจน์สมมติฐานรีมันน์แบบทั่วไปได้สำเร็จ

คู่มือนี้จะอธิบายว่าตัวตรวจสอบข้อพิสูจน์ของ Lean ตัดสินได้อย่างไรว่าอะไรคือความจริง ข้ออ้างเรื่องรีมันน์แสดงอะไรและไม่ได้แสดงอะไร และคุณจะรันข้อพิสูจน์แรกของตัวเองได้อย่างไร

Lean 4 เป็นภาษาโปรแกรมเชิงฟังก์ชันและตัวพิสูจน์ทฤษฎีบทแบบโต้ตอบ คุณประกาศทฤษฎีบทในรูปของชนิดข้อมูล (type) เขียนข้อพิสูจน์เป็นโปรแกรมที่มีชนิดข้อมูลนั้น แล้ว kernel ของ Lean จะตรวจสอบทุกขั้นตอน หาก kernel ยอมรับ ข้อพิสูจน์นั้นก็ถูกต้องตามตรรกะและสัจพจน์ของ Lean หากขั้นตอนใดล้มเหลว ไฟล์นั้นจะคอมไพล์ไม่ผ่าน

ข้อเท็จจริงบางประการจากหน้าประวัติของ Lean FRO เอง:

Lean รวมเครื่องมือสองอย่างไว้ในตัวเดียว นั่นคือ ภาษาที่คอมไพล์เป็นโค้ดเนทีฟ และตัวช่วยพิสูจน์ที่ระบบชนิดข้อมูลแบบพึ่งพา (dependent type system) ทำให้คุณพิสูจน์ได้ว่าโค้ดตรงตามสเปกสำหรับทุกอินพุต ไม่ใช่แค่เฉพาะอินพุตที่คุณทดสอบเท่านั้น

เมื่อวันศุกร์ที่ 20 พฤศจิกายน 2026 Levent Alpöge สมาชิกทีมเทคนิคของ Anthropic ได้โพสต์บันทึกความยาวสี่หน้าบนเว็บไซต์ของเขาใจความว่า "ผมเชื่อว่าผมได้ค้นพบข้อพิสูจน์ของสมมติฐานรีมันน์แล้ว โดยทำงานร่วมกับ Claude" เขาไม่ได้เผยแพร่เป็นเปเปอร์วิชาการแบบปกติ แต่เผยแพร่ข้อโต้แย้งในรูปแบบโค้ด Lean ตามรายงานของ Al Jazeera และเขียนว่า "Claude ทำได้เร็วกว่าผมมากในช่วงเข้าเส้นชัย"

ต้องทำความเข้าใจขอบเขตให้ถูก เพราะพาดหัวข่าวหลายแห่งทำไม่สำเร็จ:

ทำไม Lean จึงสำคัญในกรณีนี้? เพราะไม่มีใครอ่านโค้ด 17 ล้านบรรทัดได้หมด ข้ออ้างนี้สมควรได้รับความสนใจก็เพราะโปรแกรมขนาดเล็กที่ถูกศึกษามาอย่างดีได้ตรวจสอบโค้ดทุกบรรทัดเรียบร้อยแล้ว

Lean แบ่งงานออกเป็นส่วนหน้า (front end) ที่ไม่ต้องเชื่อถือ และส่วนหลัง (back end) ที่ต้องเชื่อถือ ความฉลาดทั้งหมดอยู่ที่ส่วนหน้า ส่วนทุกอย่างที่คุณต้องไว้ใจนั้นอยู่ใน kernel ซึ่งเว็บไซต์ของ Lean อธิบายว่าเป็น "minimal trusted kernel" (kernel ขนาดเล็กที่เชื่อถือได้)

นี่คือเหตุผลที่ข้อพิสูจน์ที่ AI เขียนสามารถเชื่อถือได้: ความพยายามส่วนใหญ่ผิด และมีเพียง term ที่ kernel ยอมรับเท่านั้นที่รอด

มีช่องทางหลบเลี่ยงสองอย่างที่ต้องระวัง sorry ช่วยให้คุณข้ามขั้นตอนใดขั้นตอนหนึ่งไปได้ และ Lean จะติดธงทุก declaration ที่ใช้มัน ส่วนสัจพจน์เพิ่มเติมช่วยให้คุณสมมติสิ่งต่างๆ ได้ คำสั่ง #print axioms จะแสดงรายการสัจพจน์ทั้งหมดที่ทฤษฎีบทนั้นพึ่งพา ผู้ตรวจสอบจึงเห็นได้ในบรรทัดเดียวว่ามีการสมมติอะไรแอบแฝงหรือไม่

นี่คือไฟล์ Lean 4 ที่สมบูรณ์ซึ่งคุณนำไปวางใน Lean playground ได้เลย:

ผู้ตรวจสอบผลลัพธ์สำคัญๆ จะเช็กสิ่งนี้ก่อนเป็นอันดับแรก: ต้องไม่มี sorry และไม่มีสัจพจน์ที่ไม่คาดคิด

การพิสูจน์ทฤษฎีบทด้วย AI ทำงานเป็นลูป โมเดลเสนอ Lean ตอบกลับ แล้วโมเดลลองใหม่ ข้อผิดพลาดและเป้าหมายที่ยังค้างอยู่ของ Lean คือฟีดแบ็ก ส่วนคำตัดสินของ kernel ถือเป็นที่สิ้นสุด

นี่คือรูปแบบเดียวกับงานรุ่นก่อนที่คุณอาจเคยอ่านผ่านตา AlphaProof ของ Google DeepMind ทำผลงานได้ในระดับเหรียญเงินของการแข่งขันคณิตศาสตร์โอลิมปิก (IMO) เมื่อเดือนกรกฎาคม 2024 โดยใช้ Lean และ Mathlib ขณะที่โมเดลโอเพนซอร์สอย่าง DeepSeek Prover V2 และ DeepSeekMath-V2 ก็ฝึกกับ Lean หรือตรวจสอบขั้นตอนของตัวเอง

Mathlib คือเหตุผลที่แนวทางนี้ขยายขนาดได้ เว็บไซต์ของ Lean อธิบายว่าเป็นไลบรารีของชุมชนที่มี "คณิตศาสตร์ที่ทำรูปนัยแล้วกว่าล้านบรรทัด" ครอบคลุมพีชคณิต การวิเคราะห์ ทอพอโลยี และความน่าจะเป็น ข้อพิสูจน์เกี่ยวกับฟังก์ชัน L ไม่ได้เริ่มจากสัจพจน์ของเลขคณิต แต่ต่อยอดจากสิ่งที่ Mathlib ตรวจสอบไว้แล้ว

นักพัฒนารู้จักแนวคิดนี้ในอีกเวอร์ชันหนึ่งที่อ่อนกว่า นั่นคือการทดสอบ

ข้อพิสูจน์อาจสมบูรณ์แบบแต่กลับพิสูจน์ข้อความที่ผิดได้ นี่คือเหตุผลที่นักคณิตศาสตร์จะใช้เวลาหลายสัปดาห์อ่านว่าโค้ด Lean ของ Alpöge ระบุอะไรไว้จริงๆ ส่วนการทดสอบพิสูจน์ได้น้อยกว่า แต่ต้นทุนต่ำและรันทุกครั้งที่คอมมิต

สำหรับการติดตั้งในเครื่อง ให้ทำตามคู่มือติดตั้งอย่างเป็นทางการ:

บทเรียนจาก Lean สำหรับทีม API นั้นง่ายมาก: เขียนสัญญาให้ชัด แล้วให้เครื่องตรวจทุกผลลัพธ์เทียบกับสัญญานั้น ในงาน API สัญญาก็คือสเปกของคุณ และการตรวจก็คือการตรวจสอบความถูกต้องของ response

Apidog ตรวจสอบ response เทียบกับสคีมาที่สเปก endpoint ของคุณประกาศไว้ ฟิลด์ที่หายไป ชนิดข้อมูลที่ผิด และพร็อพเพอร์ตี้ที่เกินมาจึงถูกตรวจพบได้โดยไม่ต้องเขียน assertion เอง Apidog CLI ช่วยให้ coding agent ของคุณรันการตรวจสอบเหล่านี้ให้ ในแบบเดียวกับที่ Claude รัน Lean เป็นลูป คุณเขียนพรอมป์ต์เดียว แล้ว agent จะอ่านสเปก เขียนเทสต์เคส และรันมันให้

จากนั้นให้พรอมป์ต์เดียวกับ Claude Code, Codex หรือ Cursor:

agent จะค้นหา endpoint และ response ที่ประกาศไว้ เขียนเทสต์เคสจากสคีมาที่ผ่านการตรวจสอบ แล้วรันทุกเคสบน endpoint นั้น:

เช่นเดียวกับ kernel ของ Lean สเปกคือผู้ตัดสิน: เมื่อแบ็กเอนด์เบี่ยงเบนไป การรันจะล้มเหลว และ agent จะบอกคุณว่าฟิลด์ไหนพัง ใส่คำสั่ง test-case run ... -r junit เดียวกันนี้ใน CI เพื่อให้ทุก pull request ถูกตรวจสอบ คู่มือ Apidog CLI สำหรับ CI/CD แสดงวิธีตั้งค่ากับ GitHub Actions และ Apidog CLI ใน Claude Code ครอบคลุมฝั่ง agent สำหรับทฤษฎีการทดสอบเบื้องหลัง ดูได้ที่ API contract testing แพ็กเกจ Free ของ Apidog รองรับผู้ใช้สูงสุด 4 คน

Lean 4 ใช้ทำอะไร? Lean 4 ใช้สำหรับทำรูปนัยคณิตศาสตร์ (Mathlib, โปรเจกต์ทฤษฎีบทสุดท้ายของแฟร์มา) ใช้ตรวจสอบซอฟต์แวร์และฮาร์ดแวร์ และใช้เป็นตัวตรวจสอบในการพิสูจน์ทฤษฎีบทด้วย AI นอกจากนี้ยังเป็นภาษาเชิงฟังก์ชันอเนกประสงค์ที่คอมไพล์เป็นโค้ดเนทีฟได้

Claude พิสูจน์สมมติฐานรีมันน์ได้จริงหรือ? Levent Alpöge กล่าวว่าเขาค้นพบข้อพิสูจน์ของสมมติฐานรีมันน์แบบทั่วไปโดยทำงานร่วมกับ Claude และเผยแพร่ในรูปแบบโค้ด Lean Lean ตรวจสอบโค้ดนั้นแล้ว แต่นักคณิตศาสตร์ยังอยู่ระหว่างทำความเข้าใจว่าโค้ด 17 ล้านบรรทัดนั้นแสดงอะไร ซึ่งคาดว่าต้องใช้เวลาหลายสัปดาห์

Lean 4 ใช้ฟรีหรือไม่? ใช่ Lean 4 และ Mathlib เป็นโอเพนซอร์ส และ Lean FRO เป็นองค์กรไม่แสวงกำไร คุณสามารถรันในเครื่องด้วย elan หรือใน playground บนเบราว์เซอร์ได้โดยไม่มีค่าใช้จ่าย

ตัวตรวจสอบข้อพิสูจน์ผิดพลาดได้ไหม? ในทางทฤษฎีได้ นี่คือเหตุผลที่ Lean เก็บ kernel ที่ต้องเชื่อถือให้เล็ก และรองรับการตรวจซ้ำอย่างอิสระด้วยเครื่องมืออย่าง Comparator ความเสี่ยงในทางปฏิบัติที่ใหญ่กว่าคือข้อความทฤษฎีบทที่ไม่ได้สื่อถึงสิ่งที่คุณตั้งใจ

ต้องรู้คณิตศาสตร์ขั้นสูงไหมจึงจะเรียน Lean 4 ได้? ไม่ต้อง เริ่มจากทฤษฎีบทง่ายๆ เกี่ยวกับจำนวนธรรมชาติและลิสต์ หรือเริ่มจาก Lean ในฐานะภาษาโปรแกรม โปรเจกต์ tutorial ของ Mathlib และ playground ถูกออกแบบมาสำหรับผู้เริ่มต้น

#9734. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)


If you want to pay online, you need to register an account and provide credit card information. If you don't have a credit card, you can pay with bank transfer. With the rise of cryptocurrencies, these methods may become old.

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain. 

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

So, What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

  • Blockchain collects information in “blocks”.
  • A block has a storage capacity, and once it's used up, it can be closed and linked to a previously served block.
  • Blocks form chains, which are called “Blockchains.”
  • More information will be added to the block with the most content until its capacity is full. The process repeats itself.
  • Each block in the chain has an exact timestamp and can't be changed.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

How does blockchain work?

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

Here’s how it works:

  • Someone or a computer will transacts
  • The transaction is transmitted throughout the network.
  • A network of computers can confirm the transaction.
  • When it is confirmed a transaction is added to a block
  • The blocks are linked together to create a history.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

  • A new transaction is added to the system. It is then relayed to a network of computers located around the world. The computers then solve equations to ensure the authenticity of the transaction.
  • Once a transaction is confirmed, it is placed in a block after the confirmation. All of the blocks are chained together to create a permanent history of every transaction.

How are Blockchains used?

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

What is Blockchain Decentralization?

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Pros and Cons of Blockchain

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages. 

Pros

  • Accuracy is increased because there is no human involvement in the verification process.
  • One of the great things about decentralization is that it makes information harder to tamper with.
  • Safe, private, and easy transactions
  • Provides a banking alternative and safe storage of personal information

Cons

  • Data storage has limits.
  • The regulations are always changing, as they differ from place to place.
  • It has a risk of being used for illicit activities 

Frequently Asked Questions About Blockchain

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Is Blockchain a cryptocurrency?

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Is it possible for Blockchain to be hacked?

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

What is the most prominent blockchain company?

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Who owns Blockchain?

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

What is the difference between Bitcoin and Blockchain technology?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency 

What is the difference between Blockchain and a Database?

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Final Saying

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9733. Hermes: reminders that carry the check

Posted on Nov 23 • Originally published at blog.hoegun.xyz

The loose end I leave most often isn't a bug. It's "check this next week."

I ship a fix, and the real test is next week's numbers. I send a partner a question, and I need to chase it on Friday if nothing comes back. A coding agent can do the work today, but in my setup the session didn't leave a durable follow-up behind, and I've learned not to assume the next session has this one's context.

My calendar notes didn't fix that either. They held a title, "check the fix", not a ready-to-run check, and a week later I had to rebuild everything else: what exactly to look at, why it mattered, and what a normal result would look like. By then the context was gone, so the check got skipped, or done badly.

This is part 7 of a series on what I learned putting AI agents to work in my own job. It's about the smallest agent I run, and the design choice that made it useful.

When I finish a task, I know four things that I won't know next week:

The fourth is the one my calendar notes never had, and it's the one that saves the most time. So the question became: where do I put a follow-up that carries all four, and who reminds me?

I went through three designs before one stuck.

First, a plain reminder from my personal assistant. Hermes is my personal assistant, a profile on the open-source Hermes Agent runtime that I talk to in a Slack DM. It reminded me on the day, but it can't see any company data, so I still had to do the whole check myself. I dropped it.

Second, a scheduled job on the team agent. kenny, the agent that answers my team's questions, can read production data through a read-only view. So I had my coding agent register a one-off scheduled job on kenny: on the day, kenny would run the check itself and post the result. It worked: a test run queried the data once and reported back.

It was also heavy. Each follow-up meant logging in to the agent host, registering the job, test-running a copy, re-baselining the integrity check that pins every scheduled job, committing, and syncing. Twice, two of my coding-agent sessions did it at once: once registering the same job forty seconds apart, once committing new baselines at the same time and having to be untangled. And I couldn't close or postpone a follow-up from Slack; that needed another round on the host.

Third, back to the assistant, on purpose. The obvious fix was to let kenny create its own jobs from a Slack conversation. I decided against it. kenny touches production data, and its guardrails deliberately stop it from changing its own configuration through chat. Giving an agent like that the power to create persistent jobs from a conversation is exactly the kind of widening I don't want. So I gave up the version that could run the check by itself, and took the smaller blast radius instead: the assistant only reminds, and I run the check.

At the end of a task, my coding agent posts one message to Hermes in Slack. It always has the same fields: a title, when to remind me first, how (once, or until I answer), and then the important part: what to check and why, what normal looks like, and a request I can paste straight back into a coding agent.

Hermes turns that into a reminder. By default it reminds me twice a day from the chosen date, up to seven times over four days, stopping sooner when I answer. When it fires, I paste the request into a local agent, which has the access Hermes doesn't, and judge the result. Then I reply in the thread with one word (in my setup the replies are Korean words; these are their translations):

That's the whole interface. Registering, finishing and postponing all happen in Slack. Nothing changes on the team agent, and nothing gets committed.

The message itself is also the record. Weeks later, the registration post says why I wanted to check, which is half of what part 5 is about.

I wrote the new rules on 8 November and moved everything the same day: four pending follow-ups and one daily reminder came off the team agent and became Hermes reminders.

Testing the reply paths that day caught a bug in "again". Replying "again" did recreate the reminder, but in the wrong mode: an "until I answer" reminder came back as a one-off, which would have fired once and then gone quiet. Hermes now has an explicit rule to keep the original mode. The lesson I keep relearning: the creation path is the one everyone tests; the reply paths are where reminders quietly die.

Speed was never the problem. When I first connected a coding agent to Hermes over Slack, the round trip from posting to a reply in the thread was 4.4 seconds. Registering a follow-up is one message my coding agent writes for me.

Hermes does one more job: I ask it for advice on decisions. One recommendation, the reason, and the cost if it's wrong. The decision stays mine.

I wanted it to reason like an experienced founder. The tempting way is to write that history into its instructions: "you've run three companies". I didn't, because a model given a fake history will produce fake anecdotes, "at my second company we...", and those read like evidence. When I'm the one making a real decision from the advice, invented evidence is the most dangerous thing it can produce.

So its instructions describe a perspective, not a past: what it looks at first, what it weighs heavily, what it's suspicious of. It speaks in patterns and judgments, never in made-up stories, and it never hides that it's an AI. The advice is a little less impressive. It's also something I can actually check.

Two follow-ups I registered on 15 and 16 November, both written by my coding agent at the end of the task:

Neither needed me to remember anything except to read a Slack message.

What's the follow-up you most often forget, and what would the reminder need to say for you to do it in five minutes?

#9732. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.
