#9612. 8 Fish With More Protein Than Salmon

Unless you've been living under a rock, you'll know that protein-maxxing is all the rage right now. The conversation largely revolves around go-to options like chicken breast, but we'll let you in on a little-known secret: Several meats out there actually outrank poultry when it comes to the macronutrient. Among them are certain types of fish, a protein source that often gets sidelined in the conversation, but leaving it out would be a serious mistake. Aside from being delicious, versatile, and (much of the time) budget-friendly, fish is also seriously easy to cook.

Salmon may be the most popular high-protein fish, and 100 grams of the farmed Atlantic variety contains around 20.3 grams of protein. That's already impressive, since it beats the 18.2 grams found in the same amount of 90% lean ground beef and comes up just under 2 grams shy of chicken breast. Compared to other fish, however, salmon actually gets outdone.

Tuna sits at or near the very top of the seafood protein hierarchy thanks to its lean, muscular build, but beyond whole fish, another serious source of protein is the canned variety. At face value, a tiny, oily anchovy isn't much to look at. But once these fish are packed tightly into cans, you're left with a surprisingly concentrated source of protein, along with a healthy dose of other beneficial nutrients. If anchovies pack too much of a punch for your taste, canned sardines also make for an excellent high-protein swap — and that's only the beginning.

Salty, briny, and often budget-friendly, canned anchovies contain a whopping 25.4 grams per 100-gram serving. You can enjoy them straight from the can since they're already cured, or if you want to take a more elevated approach, take a cue from the Portuguese and use them as an elegant garnish on toast alongside capers, good-quality olive oil, pickled red onions, and a sprinkling of parsley for good measure.

Sardines might be tiny, but they're loaded with protein (around 24 grams per 100 grams, to be precise). Like anchovies, they're an oily, nutrient-rich fish, but they set themselves apart with a milder, less salty flavor. Often sold whole, they make for a visually appealing garnish if you're looking to add a little drama to your dishes, and since canned sardines have already been cooked, they're good to eat straight out of the tin.

Yellowfin tuna, also known as ahi, is one of the more premium tuna species out there. Alongside its firm, beef-like texture and clean flavor, it's loaded with protein, with a 100-gram serving containing around 24.7 grams. It's also exceptionally versatile, since suppliers cut it into loins, saku blocks, and steaks for a hearty meal, while thinly sliced or cubed pieces work wonders in a tropical poke bowl or as delicious nigiri if you're craving something lighter.

Bluefin is the undisputed king of tuna; it's prized for sushi and sashimi, and its price can reach heights that can only be described as absurd — a 612-pound bluefin once sold for $3 million at a 2019 Tokyo auction. Like its price, its protein content sits on the higher end of the spectrum, too, reaching roughly 23 grams per 100-gram serving. But bluefin is better known for its impressive fat content, with the fatty otoro belly especially prized for its smooth, buttery texture.

Tilapia is one of the most popular fish in America, and despite its bargain price tag, it delivers a serious amount of protein, with a 100-gram serving containing 26.2 grams. It's also a solid pick if you've got sustainability in mind, since responsibly farmed tilapia can be relatively easy on the environment. This lean whitefish has a firm, flaky texture and mild flavor that stands up beautifully to grilling or pan-searing, making for a quick and satisfying weeknight dinner.

Halibut is a fan favorite that just edges out salmon's protein content, with approximately 20.8 grams per 100 grams. Despite those similar protein profiles, halibut is a lower-fat alternative with a considerably less fishy taste, making it a popular pick for those who have yet to come around on salmon. There are plenty of ways to prepare it, and grilling, pan-frying, or baking will all make for a delicious meal.

Notable for its vibrant red skin, firm white flesh, and uniquely sweet, nutty flavor, red snapper is a hugely popular seafood choice that packs 20.51 grams of protein per 100-gram serving. Compared to your everyday whitefish, its price tag ranges from moderate to expensive, but it more than makes up for it with a wonderfully tender texture. To make use of its dramatic red hue, pair your snapper with seasonings and aromatics and bake it whole.

If you've grown tired of salmon's ever-rising price tag, look no further than rainbow trout. Also available as steelhead trout, this seriously underrated fish has a milder, more delicate flavor than salmon and leaner, finer-flaked flesh. Rainbow trout contains 20.5 grams of protein per 100-gram serving, though its leaner profile makes it less forgiving than salmon at very high heat, so it's best suited to gentler methods like pan-frying or whole roasting.

#9611. Panera Is Giving Away Free Baguettes Just In Time For Thanksgiving

The bakery-café chain is giving away free baguettes on Wednesday, November 25, just in time for Thanksgiving dinner. And considering how expensive holiday grocery shopping can get, I’ll happily take a little free bread.

The giveaway is pretty straightforward: Starting at 11 a.m., customers can visit select participating Panera locations and receive a free baguette with any in-café purchase. Having an extra loaf of bread around on Thanksgiving is never a bad idea. Between soaking up leftover gravy, serving alongside dinner, and making sandwiches with whatever turkey survives the night, there are plenty of ways to put it to good use.

#9610. Forget Plain Bacon: Add This Crispy Ingredient To Grilled Cheese For Sweet & Smoky Flavor

Plain old bacon can elevate even the plainest grilled cheese, but it tends to be a bit one-note, contributing mainly salty, crispy protein. However, if you add candied bacon instead, that extra sweetness can transform a wide variety of cheeses and breads, especially if you take the time to prepare it with extra seasonings.

Candied bacon is a delicate recipe, but if you manage to make it without burning the sugars, you get an incomparably delicious ingredient for grilled cheese. The syrupy sweetness helps cut through the sodium, whether from aged parmesan or bread crusted with garlic salt, and the texture provides a nice contrast to gooey cheese. The smokiness, in particular, is a great flavoring agent that you can easily control by increasing or reducing the amount of bacon you layer on. The end result is a nice middle ground between turning grilled cheese into a dessert and keeping it exclusively savory.

Candied bacon can take a hot minute to prepare and cook, and while it only lasts about a week in the fridge, it stays good in the freezer for up to six months. Since all you have to do is let it thaw, then zap it in the air fryer for a few minutes at 380 degrees Fahrenheit, it's a superbly easy accoutrement to keep on hand for when you want something a little special.

The best part of using candied bacon is that while it may close a few flavor doors, it opens up so many more. You may not want to pair it with an herbed goat cheese or wine-veined cheddar, but it can substantially upgrade many of the tastiest underrated cheeses into something spectacular.

When considering what to add to your new sandwich, try to think about the types of cheeses you'd find in desserts. Something creamy and high in fat provides fantastic texture and an aromatic backdrop of flavor but still lets the candied bacon take center stage. Brie, Camembert, and mascarpone are all sublime with a bit of sugar, but when balanced with the savoriness of cured bacon, they become even better. Any pale, rich variety should do the job well.

You should always use a variety of cheeses in your grilled cheese, and a dash of something sharp and aged can balance out the powerful flavors of candied bacon. Microplaning some aged Manchego or provolone on top diversifies the flavors without overpowering them, and the extra-fine texture helps even harder cheeses melt more evenly. While you don't want these to be the main characters of your recipe, a bit of added nuttiness and earthiness can bring out the best in your bacon, even if you only add a tablespoon or two.

#9609. 19 non-traditional Thanksgiving desserts that aren't pie : Cakes, cookies, and even a tiramisu for your holiday dessert table.

Yes, Thanksgiving is a pie-centric holiday. But what if you don’t like pie? Or maybe you just don’t want it. Either way, we’ve got lots of non-pie Thanksgiving desserts, from spiced pumpkin cupcakes to sugary apple cobblers, plus plenty of autumnal cakes.

This adorable cake pulls double duty, serving as both a scene-stealing centerpiece and a feast-ending dessert. To make, stack two mini Bundt cakes together and frost with orange buttercream. Carving this frosted pumpkin at the end of the meal may just upstage the turkey!

Get the recipe: The Great Pumpkin Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Mini Bundt Pan Set

This dessert demonstrates how to dress up a crumb cake for fall: Top velvety sour cream cake with a juicy layer of apples, then crown the cake with a generous layer of apple pie-spiced streusel.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant Clearjel

Cranberry sauce can be a polarizing side dish, but everyone will love this New England-inspired cake, which pairs tart cranberries with walnuts and vanilla for a simple, satisfying dessert. (Because it’s so quick to make, this is a particularly good recipe for any last-minute holiday baking.)

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Sparkling Sugar

Sweet potatoes belong on the dessert table, and this recipe proves it. This ultra-soft cake is gently spiced and glows orange from the sweet potato purée, and it’s finished with a fluffy meringue that mimics marshmallow-topped sweet potato casseroles.

For a dessert that’s rich but not too sweet, turn to this recipe, which pairs pumpkin and pumpkin spice with chocolate chips. Baked in a decorative Bundt pan, it can be served unfrosted for an easy-yet-elegant dessert.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Soft Swirl Bundt Pan

Instead of apple pie, try an apple pan dowdy on your Thanksgiving dessert table. The pan dowdy is a traditional American dish from the 1800s and early 1900s. A combination of pie and pudding, the name comes from the method in which the recipe is completed: After an apple-based filling is baked in a crust-lined casserole, the baker takes a fork and "dowdies" the crust, breaking it into pieces that remain crisp despite being partially immersed in the juicy filling.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9" square pan

“Thanksgiving cheesecake” may not have quite the same ring as “Thanksgiving pie,” but when your guests are eating this ultra-creamy dessert, they won’t care. With its burnished top and custardy interior, this Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake reimagines the classic with bold autumnal flair, thanks to golden pumpkin purée and warm spices.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Golden Wheat Flour

If you don’t want to fuss with pie, we suggest making a cobbler instead. This fruit-filled version pairs juicy spiced apples with a crackly brown sugar crust — both prep and serving are easy, and the resulting cobbler will absolutely steal the show.

This holiday-ready version of our five-star Everyday Olive Oil Cake is adorned with a big red bow in the form of a simple but stunning cranberry glaze. Made by cooking cranberries with orange juice, then whisking the mixture with confectioners’ sugar, the icing adds a bright tartness that complements the rich cake.

Get the recipe: Cranberry-Orange Olive Oil Cake

#9608. Skip Soy Sauce: Marinate Steak In This Umami Ingredient For A Delicious Flavor Boost

People love soy sauce for a next-level steak marinade not just because of its salt, but also its complexity. If, however, you want to eschew the sodium and bump up that deliciously fermented flavor, you need koji, a type of rice critical to Japanese sake production.

When you inoculate short-grain rice with Aspergillus oryzae mold, it slowly breaks down proteins and carbohydrates into an ingredient you can then ferment for sake or dry for use as a savory, shelf-stable ingredient. This is koji, a lesser-known source of umami that is nonetheless a potent marinade ingredient. While the differences are more subtle than with soy sauce, it gives you great control over your meat's final flavor profile and leaves you room to add other seasonings, like the best salts for seasoning steak, herbs, and spices.

If you use shio koji, a type of marinade made by combining koji rice with salt and water, you can even tenderize your meat. The sodium helps the beef retain moisture, while the enzymes break down proteins, leaving your steak tender and flavorful no matter how you prepare it. Just be careful, as some varieties have added sugars that can unexpectedly sweeten your meat too much. While they won't exactly candy your steak, they might overhaul your food's taste.

Whether you use wet shio koji or dry, shelf-stable koji, this ingredient is extremely useful and easy to add to marinades. Just keep in mind that its enzymes remain active when wet, so you'll want to be careful about how long you let your steak sit before cooking.

Dry, shelf-stable koji is quite versatile but may require extra steps. Grinding it into a powder and adding a few tablespoons to your marinade is a great way to boost umami. However, you can also create a dry crust on your steak and let it sit in your fridge for a couple of days. This can mimic some of the effects of long dry-aging, helping your beef develop an impressive level of complexity in only 48 hours. However, you'll want to rinse the rice off your meat and pat it dry before cooking, as its starches and natural sugars burn quite easily.

Shio koji is a bit easier to use and so delicious that you don't even need other marinade ingredients. Since it's able to thoroughly coat the meat, this is a great choice if you're working with tough cuts, like flank steak, that need some extra tenderizing. Two tablespoons per pound of protein should be plenty to get tender meat. To get a good crust, you'll still want to wipe off the excess rice and moisture and watch your heat, but it's an otherwise hands-off recipe that can taste like you spent hours fretting over the perfect marinade.
